Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache status ignores cache expiry

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds groups all CalendarCache rows by credentialId with no expiresAt filter, whereas getCachedAvailability only serves rows with expiresAt >= now. Credentials whose only cache entries are expired (up to a month old, no longer served) will still be reported as having cache, so the UI displays a 'Last updated' status and offers deletion for data that is already unusable, and the timestamp does not reflect any live cache.

Delete-cache mutation never refreshes connectedCalendars data

The deleteCacheMutation onSuccess only shows a toast and calls the optional external onSuccess callback. Unlike the disconnect mutation in the same file (onSettled invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars), it never invalidates that query, and SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper's own query is not refetched by the external onChanged callback. After a successful deletion the dropdown therefore keeps showing the old cacheUpdatedAt timestamp and 'Delete cached data' action until a manual reload, making it look like the deletion did nothing.

Handler bypasses the calendar-cache repository abstraction and always queries

The handler directly instantiates the concrete CalendarCacheRepository on every connectedCalendars call, instead of going through the CalendarCache/calendar-cache-disabled path that CalendarCacheRepositoryMock exists for. This adds a groupBy query to every connected-calendars load (including users with no Google credentials and orgs with calendar-cache disabled, where the mock would return []) and surfaces cache status/deletion for stale rows even when the cache feature is off.

Pre-existing cache rows get migration time as updatedAt

Adding updatedAt as NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW() stamps every legacy CalendarCache row with the migration/deployment time rather than its actual last-write time. Immediately after deploy, the new UI will present that deployment timestamp as 'Cache last updated' for all existing credentials, even for cache entries written weeks earlier, giving users a misleading freshness signal until each row happens to be rewritten.

dev:cron now depends on unpinned npx tsx which is not a declared dependency

tsx is not listed in apps/web (or root) dependencies, so `npx tsx cron-tester.ts` will download an unpinned package from the registry on first run. That breaks offline/air-gapped dev environments, is a supply-chain risk, and can silently change behavior as tsx releases change; tsx should be added as a pinned devDependency or the previously available ts-node kept.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellations are fired without awaiting persistence of the cancelled flag

updatedBookings.forEach(...) calls the async deleteScheduledEmailReminder/deleteScheduledSMSReminder and discards the returned promises. The handler then deletes attendees/references, sends cancellation emails and returns 200 without guaranteeing the prisma update that sets cancelled=true (or the SMS/Twilio cancellation and row deletion) has completed. In a serverless/short-lived invocation the process can finish or be frozen before the update lands, leaving the reminder active for the cron/SendGrid to send; the same un-awaited pattern in the try/catch in handleNewBooking.ts also means that try/catch can never observe failures. These promises should be collected and awaited (e.g. Promise.all) before responding.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path leaves the reminder row active with no retry if SendGrid fails

When immediateDelete is true, deleteScheduledEmailReminder issues the SendGrid cancel request and returns without deleting the WorkflowReminder row and without setting cancelled=true. The reschedule caller in handleNewBooking.ts relies on this path and does not delete the old booking's reminders via cascade, so the old row remains scheduled=true/cancelled=null; the cron job only retries rows with cancelled=true, so if the SendGrid request throws (the error is only logged inside this function) nothing ever retries the cancellation and the old booking's reminder email is still sent. It also leaves stale scheduled reminder rows attached to the superseded booking until their scheduledDate passes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Last-minute cancellations are deleted without ever cancelling the SendGrid email

Deferred cancellation only happens when the cron job runs and finds cancelled=true with scheduledDate within the next hour, but at the top of the same handler all EMAIL workflowReminders with scheduledDate <= now are deleted unconditionally before the cancellation block runs. If a booking is cancelled after the last cron run before its reminder's send time (the PR states the cron runs every 15 minutes), the next run can cross the scheduledDate, delete the DB row first, and never issue the SendGrid cancel for that batch; SendGrid has already dispatched the email. The reminder for a just-cancelled booking is therefore still sent in this window, and the row deletion removes any chance of a later retry.

One failed SendGrid cancellation aborts cancellation of all remaining reminders

The entire cancellation loop is wrapped in a single try/catch and each SendGrid request is awaited inside it. If cancelling one reminder fails (for example an invalid or already-cancelled batch_id), the exception exits the loop, the remaining reminders in the next-hour window are never sent a cancellation request, and the Prisma delete operations already queued in workflowRemindersToDelete are never awaited (they are lazy Prisma promises), so even successfully-cancelled reminders keep their rows. Those uncancelled SendGrid emails will still be delivered for cancelled/rescheduled bookings. Each reminder needs its own error handling so one failure does not block the rest.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async forEach makes calendar/video cancellation fire-and-forget and bypasses try/catch

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) })` discards the promises returned by the callback. Reschedule() can return true and the reschedule email can be sent before deletions finish, deletions can be lost on process termination, and a rejection from the now-async getCalendar/deleteMeeting is not caught by the surrounding try/catch (which only catches synchronous throws), producing an unhandled rejection instead of the logged error. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` inside the try.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are all executed eagerly, not lazily per app

Every value in the appStore object literal is an import() call, so merely importing packages/app-store/index.ts immediately starts loading all ~30 app modules; accessing appStore.zoomvideo does not lazily load only Zoom. This defeats the stated goal of async/lazy app loading, keeps the startup/bundle cost the PR aims to remove, and creates stored promises for apps that are never used (including possible unhandled rejections if an unused app fails to load). Values should be thunks such as `zoomvideo: () => import("./zoomvideo")` and call sites should invoke then await them.

requestReschedule does not await calendar/video deletions

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) / deleteMeeting(...) })` discards the async callback promises. The mutation proceeds to send the reschedule email and webhooks and returns without guaranteeing the old calendar/video events were deleted, and any rejection from getCalendar/deleteEvent/deleteMeeting becomes an unhandled rejection rather than being surfaced or logged. Replace forEach with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours guard uses slot start twice and lets non-working days pass

In the workingHours.find callback, both start and end are computed from slotStartTime.hour()/minute(), so a slot starting inside working hours but ending after workingHour.endTime is accepted. Additionally, find only returns true when a working hour exists for slotStartTime.day() and the slot is outside it: if no working hour includes that weekday at all, or another same-day range covers the slot while an earlier range does not, the logic either falls through to the busy check as available or incorrectly rejects. This defeats the new fixed-host filtering for hosts whose hours end earlier, who don't work that day, or who have split ranges.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs object identity comparison never detects empty overrides

dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...) compares two distinct Dayjs objects by reference, so it is always false. The branch intended to recognize a zero-length override (start equals end, i.e. unavailable for that override period/day) is dead code, and such overrides are not handled as intended.

false_positives.candidate:
Date-override path bypasses busy-time checks

When a slot falls inside a date override, dateOverrideExist is set to true and checkIfIsAvailable returns true at line 135 without reaching the busy.every(...) check at line 153. Consequently calendar events and existing Cal bookings are ignored for every slot on an override day, so a fixed or round-robin host can be double-booked on days with a date override.

No test covers round-robin fixed-host date overrides

The only added test re-queries a single-user event (hosts: []) with a different invitee timezone. It does not create a ROUND_ROBIN event with a fixed host and a loose host, does not give only the fixed host a date override, and does not exercise the new checkIfIsAvailable dateOverrides/workingHours filtering added for fixed/loose hosts in slots.ts. The main scenario described in the PR (slots must be limited by the fixed host's override) can regress without any test failing.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sender check crashes for integrations whose metadata has no sender

The new check unconditionally indexes integration.metadata['sender']['login']. Integrations created through this pipeline itself do not get a sender (build_integration only sets metadata['sender'] from state['sender'], which this pipeline never binds; test_basic_flow asserts metadata without 'sender'), and older integrations likewise may lack it. If such an Integration exists but has no OrganizationIntegration (e.g. the org link was removed and the installation is retried/moved to another org), installations_exist is False, this branch is reached, and a KeyError/TypeError produces a 500 instead of completing or showing the installation-failed page.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
Sender validation is bypassed when the Integration does not exist yet

When Integration.objects.get() raises DoesNotExist, GitHubInstallation immediately calls pipeline.next_step() without comparing pipeline state 'github_authenticated_user' against the GitHub user who installed the app. That row is normally created asynchronously by the GitHub installation webhook, so completion races the webhook: a user who reaches this step before the webhook is processed (or if it is delayed/lost) finishes the pipeline and build_integration() creates the integration from the installation_id alone. This defeats the PR's stated guarantee that the authenticated GitHub user must match the app installer whenever the webhook has not already created the Integration.

Token exchange and user lookup exceptions escape as 500s instead of the failure page

safe_urlopen() on line 423 is called outside the try/except (which only covers safe_urlread/parse_qsl), and get_user_info() on line 434 is also unguarded. A network error, timeout, or HTTP error from GitHub's token endpoint, or a failed /user request for a bad/expired token, will therefore raise out of OAuthLoginView.dispatch and return a 500. This contradicts the PR description that a wrong or reused 'code' (and by extension a failed token/user exchange) should show the 'Invalid installation request' error page.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the installation-not-found path

The rewritten test's second request uses state 'ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05', which fails OAuthLoginView's pipeline-signature check before GitHubInstallation/build_integration ever queries GitHub for the installation. The assertion of 'Invalid installation request.' therefore passes via the state-mismatch branch, and the stubbed 404 from /app/installations/{id} and the 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' handling in build_integration are no longer covered by any test.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource.queued is evaluated once at import time

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` calls timezone.now() when the dataclass class is defined, not when an instance is created. Every AssignmentSource created without an explicit queued value therefore shares the process import timestamp. If queued is intended to record when an assignment was queued (e.g. for future staleness/debouncing checks or observability), it will be wrong by however long the process has been running. Use field(default_factory=timezone.now) instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
to_dict() puts a raw datetime into Celery task kwargs, breaking the round-trip

assignment_source.to_dict() uses dataclasses.asdict(), so the `queued` value passed in the sync_assignee_outbound Celery kwargs is a datetime object, not a JSON-native value. Sentry Celery tasks serialize kwargs as JSON, so enqueueing can fail with a serialization error on exactly the inbound-assignment path this PR enables (propagating synchronously out of GroupAssignee.assign/deassign via sync_group_assignee_outbound), and where a serializer does coerce datetimes it arrives at AssignmentSource.from_dict as a string, silently violating the declared datetime type since from_dict performs no parsing/validation. Serialize queued to an ISO string in to_dict and parse it back in from_dict, or drop it from the wire format; the added tests use eager tasks and a direct to_dict assertion, so they never exercise this round-trip.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
No test for deassign suppression or for propagation to a different integration

The only cycle-suppression test covers assign() where the source integration matches the single linked integration, asserting the outbound call is skipped. There is no equivalent test for deassign() with a matching AssignmentSource, and no test where an assignment sourced from one integration still syncs outbound to a different linked integration, which is the behavior the should_sync comment claims to preserve. A regression that suppresses all outbound syncs whenever any assignment_source is present, or that fails to suppress deassign cycles, would pass the current suite.

Task unconditionally passes new assignment_source kwarg to all installations

sync_assignee_outbound now always calls installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source), even when it is None, while the abstract IssueSyncIntegration.sync_assignee_outbound signature was not updated to declare this parameter (it still only documents **kwargs). Any installation whose concrete sync_assignee_outbound does not accept **kwargs/an assignment_source parameter will raise TypeError at runtime, causing the task to retry and the outbound sync to fail; the new test mocks ExampleIntegration.sync_assignee_outbound, which accepts arbitrary kwargs, so it cannot catch such an incompatibility. Either declare the parameter on the abstract method and update implementations, or only pass it when supported/non-None.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated

MetricAlertDetectorHandler now extends StatefulDetectorHandler but implements none of its abstract members (counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the newly added build_occurrence_and_event_data). Detector.detector_handler does `group_type.detector_handler(self)`, so any Detector with type `metric_alert_fire` will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class ...` instead of the previous no-op handler returning an empty result. process_detectors has no exception handling around handler construction/evaluation, so this can abort processing for the whole batch.

true_positives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Stateful evaluate docstring still says it returns a list

StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate now returns `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but its docstring at line 230 still says it returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult. This misdocuments the new contract that this PR is explicitly changing for callers and subclass authors.

true_positives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mock occurrence builder ignores value so tests cannot verify value propagation

build_mock_occurrence_and_event accepts `value` but never uses it when constructing the IssueOccurrence or event_data. Consequently the new build_occurrence_and_event_data hook's most important input is unverified: several tests even build the expected occurrence with the wrong value (e.g. test_state_results_multi_group builds group_2's expected occurrence with 6 instead of the packet value 10, and TestEvaluate builds expectations with 6 for packet values 100/8) yet still pass. A regression that passed the wrong value to the hook would not be caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Converted monitor config is discarded in environment context

get_monitor_environment_context copies monitor.config into the local `config` variable and converts `config["schedule_type"]` to its display value, but the returned context uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of the converted `config`. The conversion therefore has no effect and the occurrence context continues to contain the raw schedule_type value rather than the intended display value.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hung spawn flusher is never killed before being replaced

Flusher workers are created with multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, whose objects are SpawnProcess/BaseProcess instances, not instances of multiprocessing.Process. The isinstance check therefore never passes in production, so a worker detected as hung is not killed before _create_process_for_shards starts its replacement. The hung worker can keep polling and flushing the same Redis shards concurrently with the new worker, causing duplicate buffered-segment production and races between flush_segments/done_flush_segments, while the reference to the leaked worker is overwritten in self.processes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

false_positives.candidate:
Invalid --flusher-processes values are silently remapped or crash obscurely

The CLI option added for process-spans accepts any integer and SpanFlusher performs no positive-value validation. Passing 0 is silently changed by `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` into one process per shard, the opposite of an operator's explicit request, while a negative value makes num_processes negative, builds an empty process_to_shards_map, and then fails with a KeyError on `i % self.num_processes` during shard assignment instead of a clear configuration error at startup.

join() never terminates spawn flusher processes

For the same reason as the restart path, isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is false for processes created through the spawn context (and for the threading.Thread workers used when produce_to_pipe is set, terminate is inapplicable). After join() waits until its deadline for workers that ignore the shared stopped flag, the terminate call is skipped, so shutdown can return while daemon flusher processes are still alive flushing segments and producing to Kafka; they are only cleaned up implicitly when the parent process exits.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Committable-offset scan is O(range) every second per partition

get_committable_offsets() runs min()/max() over the full all_offsets set and then iterates range(start, max_offset+1) with set lookups, and mark_committed() rebuilds the whole set - all repeated every 1s by _commit_loop for every partition. With a backlog (made likely by the unbounded queues), a single slow offset pins a large outstanding set, so each tick rescans an ever-growing range, giving quadratic behaviour and burning a thread. Track the next-expected offset and a completed set per partition instead of rescanning the whole window.

Kafka commit function is invoked from a background thread

_commit_loop runs on a dedicated daemon thread and calls self.commit_function(committable) (which is Arroyo's Commit callable built in create_thread_queue_parallel_worker) concurrently with the StreamProcessor main thread that owns submit()/poll()/close(). Arroyo commit callbacks are expected to be invoked from the processing thread during submit/poll/join; racing them against processor-driven commits and shutdown can corrupt/interleave offset state and commit offsets for partitions that have since been revoked. Perform commits from poll() on the strategy thread, using the tracker only to compute committable offsets.

Queue pool is created once in the factory but killed by each strategy close

FixedQueuePool is constructed a single time in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ (line 133) and the same instance is handed to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy from create_with_partitions(). Arroyo calls create_with_partitions() again after a rebalance/revocation, but the previous strategy's close()/terminate() calls queue_pool.shutdown(), which shuts down the shared queues and joins the workers. The next strategy reuses that dead pool: work_queue.put() raises queue.ShutDown, which SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() catches and converts into add_offset+complete_offset, so messages are silently dropped yet committed. Create a fresh pool per create_with_partitions() call (or make the pool restartable and don't shut it down in strategy close).

Queues are unbounded despite claimed backpressure

FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with the default maxsize=0 (unbounded), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() never blocks or rejects. The docstring at lines 253-254 promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but under a slow result_processor the Arroyo processor will keep submitting messages indefinitely, growing memory without bound and building a huge outstanding-offset set (also delaying commits past max.poll.interval). Bound the queues and make submit() apply backpressure, or remove the claim and add another flow-control mechanism.

Shutdown abandons queued-but-unprocessed items

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True for every worker before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker.run() re-checks `while not self.shutdown` after each item, so a worker that finishes its current item exits even if its queue still holds pending items (which immediate=False was supposed to drain). Those items are never processed and their offsets stay outstanding forever in this process; graceful shutdown silently drops in-flight work (only redelivery on restart saves it, and only if offsets were not already marked complete). Don't set the flag until queues are drained, or have workers exit only when the queue is empty and shut down.

close() stops the commit loop before workers drain

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread first, and only then calls queue_pool.shutdown(). Any items the workers finish during pool shutdown therefore complete their offsets after the last _commit_loop iteration, so those offsets are never passed to commit_function. Arroyo will consider the strategy closed and will not poll again, so successfully processed messages are redelivered and reprocessed on restart. Drain the pool first (and run a final commit pass), then stop the commit thread.

hash() is not a stable consistent hash for group assignment

get_queue_for_group() uses Python's builtin hash(group_key) % num_queues and documents it as 'consistent hashing'. For str keys hash() is randomised per process via PYTHONHASHSEED, so the group->queue mapping changes on every restart and differs between concurrently running consumer processes; it is also a plain modulo, so changing num_queues (--max-workers) remaps nearly every group. This defeats any cross-restart/cross-process affinity expectations and makes queue distribution non-reproducible in tests/operations. Use a stable digest (e.g. hashlib.md5/sha1 of the key) modulo num_queues.

submit() marks messages complete and committable on any error

The bare `except Exception` in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() logs and then does add_offset()+complete_offset() for the message regardless of where the failure occurred - e.g. grouping_fn raising, or FixedQueuePool.submit() failing after add_offset() when putting onto a shut-down queue. Combined with OrderedQueueWorker.run() completing offsets in its `finally` block even when result_processor raises (line 148-149), this contradicts the documented 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and turns transient/poison failures into committed, never-retried message loss instead of letting Arroyo/DLQ handle them. Only skip-and-commit for explicitly undecodable/filtered payloads; propagate or leave outstanding other failures.

wait_until_empty reports empty while items are still being processed

wait_until_empty() (and poll()'s total_queued gauge) rely on queue.qsize(), but OrderedQueueWorker removes an item from the queue via get() before it starts processing it. The method therefore returns True while the last item(s) - one per queue - are still in-flight and their offsets not yet completed, so any caller using it as a drain/flush barrier (as shutdown-style tests do) can proceed/commit/tear down too early. Track in-flight counts (e.g. queue.task_done()/join() or an explicit counter incremented on submit and decremented in the worker's finally).

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every cached non-allow now triggers a full database permission load

If cached permissions do not allow the request, Check always calls getIdentityPermissions, which reloads identifiers/basic role/teams (subject to their caches) and queries the permission store and rewrites permCache. The denial cache only helps exact repeats of the same action/name/parent; probing or legitimately checking many distinct resources a user cannot access bypasses it and amplifies each check into a DB query. This removes the negative-case protection previously provided by permCache and creates an easy DB load path via enumeration of resource UIDs.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous underscore-concatenation of variable fields

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, userUID, action, name and parent with '_' separators and no escaping or length encoding. Distinct tuples can produce the same key, e.g. name='a_b', parent='c' versus name='a', parent='b_c' (UIDs may contain underscores). A denial recorded for one dashboard/folder can therefore incorrectly deny a different resource for the denial TTL.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Denials caused by a stale folder tree are cached as authoritative denials

When the fresh-permission check fails, Check unconditionally writes permDenialCache. checkPermission/checkInheritedPermissions can fail solely because buildFolderTree returned the 30s-cached folder tree that does not yet contain a newly created or moved parent folder. Such a transient, infrastructure-staleness denial is then stored under the denial key and short-circuits later checks even after the folder tree and permissions have refreshed, extending incorrect denial and undermining the stated goal of letting creators access newly created folders/dashboards promptly in inherited-permission cases.

List still trusts stale cached permissions and never re-queries on outdated cache

Unlike Check, List returns listPermission directly from getCachedIdentityPermissions whenever a permCache entry exists, regardless of whether that entry predates a newly created dashboard/folder or a new grant. Because the client-side cache was removed in this PR, callers will reach this server List more often but can still omit newly accessible resources for the full shortCacheTTL (30s). The PR goal of fetching newly created dashboards/folders therefore remains broken for list/fetch flows that rely on List rather than a single Check.

Stale denial cache takes precedence over fresher permission cache

Check returns a cached denial before consulting permCache, and no code invalidates permDenialCache when fresh permissions are loaded (for example by List calling getIdentityPermissions and repopulating permCache). If a user is denied, is then granted access, and any path refreshes permCache with the new grant, Check for the same namespace/user/action/name/parent still returns Allowed:false until the denial TTL expires. This can make List show a resource while Check denies it and reintroduces up to 30s of stale denial for permission grants.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Grafana rule list items are rendered without a React key

The grafana branch returns <GrafanaRuleListItem> without the `key={key}` that GrafanaRuleLoader had and that the datasource branch still has. FilterView appends pages and batches of rules over time, so React will reconcile these items by index; component-local state in RuleActionsButtons/AlertRuleMenu (delete modal, silence drawer, clone redirect) can be reused for a different rule and list updates will be inefficient/incorrect. Restore key={key} on GrafanaRuleListItem.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence drawer never opens for prom-only Grafana rules

AlertRuleMenu can now show Silence based on the Grafana prom-rule ability and calls handleSilence, which sets showSilenceDrawer=true. The drawer itself is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true, but the new list view passes only promRule and leaves `rule` undefined. Clicking 'Silence notifications' in the list view therefore does nothing instead of opening SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete action can never appear in the ruler-less list view

canDelete is now computed as ruler-ability OR Grafana prom-rule ability, but rendering is still gated by `canDelete && rulerRule`. In the new list view RuleActionsButtons.V2/GrafanaRuleListItem pass only promRule and no rulerRule, so Delete never renders there even for users with delete permission, despite the new prom-rule ability check. The Grafana-prom delete branch is dead code; the guard (or the handleDelete contract, which currently requires a RulerRuleDTO) must be adapted for prom-only rules.

Federated rule groups lose their immutable protection

useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously computed isFederated via isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) and treated federated rules as immutable (Update/Delete/Pause unsupported). It now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, where isFederated is hardcoded to false with a TODO. CombinedRule consumers will therefore offer edit/delete/pause for federated (cross-tenant Mimir) rule groups that must not be edited this way, leading to enabled actions that should be unsupported and will fail or act on the wrong tenant scope.

Pause action can never appear in the ruler-less list view

canPause is now computed as ruler-ability OR Grafana prom-rule ability, but the menu item is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` is true and it renders MenuItemPauseRule with that rulerRule. In the new list view no rulerRule is supplied, so Pause is always hidden for Grafana rules even when the prom-rule ability allows it, making the newly added grafanaPauseAbility check ineffective for this action.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Queries that interpolate to an empty expression are no longer dropped

The empty check runs on the raw expression before interpolation: .filter((query) => query.expr).map((query) => datasource.applyTemplateVariables(...)), with no re-filter afterwards (the same ordering is used in shardQuerySplitting.ts:49-52). A target whose expression is only a template variable, e.g. expr: '$expr', passes the raw check but can interpolate to '' when the variable has no value; it is then classified by isLogsQuery/querySupportsSplitting, grouped, and sent to Loki as an empty query instead of being skipped like a directly-empty query, producing backend parse errors for the whole panel request. Filter again after applyTemplateVariables (or interpolate first, then filter).

Shard-split queries are interpolated twice

runShardSplitQuery now calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables for every target, and the resulting sub-requests are then passed to runSplitQuery, which at querySplitting.ts:299 calls applyTemplateVariables again for the same targets (the updated shard test even expects 5 calls for 1 initial query plus 4 shard sub-requests). Loki's applyTemplateVariables is not guaranteed idempotent: it applies request.filters/ad-hoc filters to the expression in addition to replacing variables, so a second pass can append the same ad-hoc label/filter twice, and any variable value containing a '$'-expression can be re-expanded. Shard splitting should interpolate only once, either here or in runSplitQuery, not both.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a detached logger that discards log records

FromContext returns NewTestLogger(), a fresh instance unrelated to the receiver. LoggerMiddleware now logs via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so any test that injects a TestLogger into LoggerMiddleware and then asserts on that instance's InfoLogs (calls/message/context) will observe nothing: the log record is counted on the throwaway logger returned here. The fake should return the receiver (or a logger sharing the same Logs state) so tests can observe logs emitted through FromContext.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

false_positives.candidate:
New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no test coverage for the moved contextual-logging behavior

This PR moves responsibility for enriching the request context with endpoint/pluginId/dsName/dsUID/uname from MetricsMiddleware into the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware, and LoggerMiddleware now depends on that enrichment via logger.FromContext(ctx) instead of adding those fields itself. No test was added for ContextualLoggerMiddleware (there is no contextual_logger_middleware_test.go), and the renamed metrics test only verifies Prometheus metrics. If the new middleware is mis-ordered in CreateMiddlewares, fails to enrich the context, or drops a field, the 'Plugin Request Completed' log line silently loses plugin/endpoint/datasource/user context with no failing test.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device-limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert race

CreateOrUpdateDevice runs CountDevices in one DB session, drops back to application code, and then inserts in a separate session with no transaction, unique constraint enforcement, or inter-instance lock. Concurrent requests (including from multiple Grafana instances sharing one database) when the count is limit-1 can all observe count < limit and all insert, exceeding the configured limit. The count check and insert/update need to be atomic, e.g. performed in a single transaction with appropriate locking.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device-limit rejection is cached, allowing the rejected device on its next request

tagDeviceUI inserts the device ID into localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice and does not remove the entry when that call returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. The first request from a new device over the limit is rejected, but for the next 29 minutes TagDevice sees the cache entry and returns nil, so Anonymous.Authenticate succeeds for the same over-limit device. The cache should only be populated after a successful store write (or evicted on error).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
New device_limit option is not declared in defaults/sample config or docs

AnonymousDeviceLimit is read from auth.anonymous device_limit, but the PR adds no entry to conf/defaults.ini or conf/sample.ini and no documentation for [auth.anonymous] device_limit. Operators have no discoverable way to learn the option exists, its unit/scope (distinct devices seen in 30 days), or that 0 means unlimited, so the headline configurable feature is effectively undocumented.

No test covers an already-known device being allowed when the limit is reached

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a second, new device is rejected. It does not verify the other half of the new contract in updateDevice: that re-tagging the existing device while count >= limit succeeds and updates it, nor that an expired device is rejected. A regression in the UPDATE ... BETWEEN window or in dialect-specific RowsAffected handling would incorrectly lock out legitimate existing anonymous devices and would not be caught.

Provider signature changes are not reflected in the generated Wire code

ProvideAnonDBStore changed from (db.DB) to (db.DB, int64) and ProvideAnonymousDeviceService changed from accepting anonstore.AnonStore to db.DB, but no wire_gen.go/wire set file is updated in this PR. The checked-in generated server wiring still calls these providers with the old arguments, so the server package will not compile until wire is regenerated and the generated file is committed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Normal cleanup batches are logged at Error level with full ID lists

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags call r.log.Error for every batch (including successful batches, an empty final batch, and cases where the logged err is nil at line 534). Routine successful cleanup will therefore generate error-level log noise/alerts, and including the entire ids slice (potentially tens of thousands of IDs with a large batch size) makes each message very large. These should be Debug/Info-level summaries without dumping all IDs.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute for all jobs

The ticker in CleanUpService.Run is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, but this ticker drives srv.clean(), which runs every cleanup job (expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, and query history), not just annotation cleanup. This increases the frequency and database/filesystem load of all of those jobs tenfold without any justification in the PR description and can worsen the MySQL contention the PR is trying to reduce.

false_positives.candidate:
Placeholder-limit workaround only handles SQLite

deleteByIDs builds one '?' placeholder per ID for every non-SQLite database, bounded only by AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize. The new large-batch test uses a batch size of 32767; on databases with prepared-statement placeholder limits (notably PostgreSQL's 65535 limit is only about twice that, and deployments can configure an even larger batch size), a sufficiently large configured batch will now fail with a parameter-limit error, whereas the previous subquery DELETE did not pass IDs as parameters at all. The check also uses the configured batch size rather than len(ids). Either inline IDs or chunk deletes based on the actual ID count for all dialects with limits.

Split fetch/delete can over-delete annotations kept by the MaxCount rule

For MaxCount cleanup, fetchIDs selects IDs using LIMIT batch OFFSET MaxCount at one instant, then deleteByIDs deletes those IDs in a separate statement/session without rechecking that they are still beyond MaxCount. If annotations that were within the newest MaxCount are deleted concurrently between the fetch and the delete, some fetched annotations may no longer be excess and should now be retained, but they will still be deleted. The previous single DELETE evaluated the excess condition atomically in one statement.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records object name in the metric kind label

On successful Delete the code calls d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage), passing the object `name` where every other call site passes options.Kind as the kind label. This creates one metric series per deleted object name (unbounded label cardinality in Prometheus) and makes per-kind aggregation impossible. It should pass options.Kind like the error path at line 103.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy calls race on objects shared with the returned response

Create passes the same `obj` pointer to Storage.Create and then to the background Legacy.Create while returning `created` to the caller, and Update passes the same `objInfo` (line 139) to both Storage.Update and the background Legacy.Update. The API server may serialise/mutate the returned object, and UpdatedObjectInfo.UpdatedObject may be invoked a second time against a different old object, concurrently with the first call and with response handling. This is a data race and can make the legacy copy differ from the object written to unified storage; the legacy goroutine needs its own deep copy / the precomputed updated object (as the previous updateWrapper approach provided).

Async legacy writes inherit the cancelled request context

Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection all launch `go func()` blocks that derive their timeout with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` from the incoming request context. The Kubernetes request context is cancelled as soon as the handler returns the storage result, which happens immediately after spawning the goroutine, so the legacy write will almost always run with an already-cancelled context and fail/abandon. A detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) before adding the timeout) is required, otherwise mode 3 silently does not perform the legacy writes it exists to perform as a safety net.

Independent goroutines give no ordering for legacy writes

Every write spawns an unsynchronised goroutine for the legacy store. A Create goroutine, a subsequent Update goroutine and a Delete goroutine for the same object can be scheduled or complete out of order (legacy latency is variable up to the 10s timeout): an update can run before the create it depends on and fail as not-found, or a delayed create can run after a delete and resurrect a deleted object in legacy storage. Mode 3 therefore can leave legacy permanently diverged from unified storage; legacy writes need to be serialised/queued per resource or otherwise ordered.

Legacy write failures are never logged

The background goroutines in Create, Delete (line 112), Update (line 139) and DeleteCollection (line 165) discard the legacy error except for a duration metric; the previous synchronous implementation logged these errors. Combined with the fire-and-forget design, an operator has no log signal (with kind/name) that legacy has diverged from unified storage and no way to know which objects need reconciliation. The error branch should log via the request-scoped logger before recording the metric.

Mode 3 tests never verify the async legacy write happens

The Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection tests register legacy mock expectations but return and assert on the storage result immediately, without waiting for the spawned goroutine or calling AssertExpectations/AssertCalled on the legacy mock (both mocks also share a single testify mock.Mock, so expectations cannot even distinguish the two stores). The tests pass even if the legacy write is removed entirely, and if the goroutine fires after the test finishes it can race with later tests using the shared mock and shared example objects. Tests need a synchronisation point (channel/WaitGroup in the mock or Eventually-style assertion) proving legacy is invoked with the right arguments.

New mode 3 integration cases are flaky because legacy visibility is now asynchronous

The added 'mode 3' subtests reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates/updates/deletes via the k8s API and then immediately asserts the objects are visible (and later gone) through the legacy /api/playlists endpoints. In mode 3 the legacy write is performed by a fire-and-forget goroutine started before the response returns, so there is no guarantee it has completed when the very next legacy request is made. These subtests will intermittently fail (missing/extra/stale playlists) unless the legacy assertions poll/wait for eventual consistency.

Storage failures are recorded as legacy metrics

In Create, when d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) with the storage start time, and Update does the same at line 129. Storage failures are therefore attributed to the legacy duration metric (with the wrong latency) and no failing storage duration is recorded, corrupting the dual-writer dashboards/alerts used to judge migration safety. These should call recordStorageDuration. Conversely DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration for the legacy call, the mirror-image mistake.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write lock is taken without re-checking the cache

In non-Dev mode, concurrent callers that all observe a nil cache under the read lock will queue on the write lock. After the first caller populates entryPointAssetsCache, each queued caller still re-reads and re-parses assets-manifest.json and replaces the cache because the non-nil check is not repeated after acquiring Lock. This serializes redundant file I/O under the exclusive lock during the initial request burst and blocks fast-path readers; re-check entryPointAssetsCache after Lock (for non-Dev) and return it if populated.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
No concurrent test covers the claimed race fix

The change adds mutex synchronization around the package-global entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test exercising concurrent GetWebAssets calls (e.g. run with -race against a temporary assets-manifest.json). Without such a regression test, a future refactor that accesses the cache outside entryPointAssetsCacheMu would not be caught by CI.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false and can dereference a nil toggle source

enableSqlExpressions computes enabled as the negation of IsEnabledGlobally, returns false when that value is true, and also returns false otherwise, so the feature-toggle check is dead logic that always disables SQL while obscuring the intent. It also dereferences h.features unconditionally for SQL queries; an ExpressionQueryReader constructed with a nil FeatureToggles (as test or auxiliary callers may do) will now panic instead of returning an error. Simplify this to an explicit unconditional return false (with a security comment) or handle a nil toggle source.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
Legacy SQL command path is not explicitly disabled

UnmarshalSQLCommand is a separate entry point from ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery and does not check whether SQL expressions are disabled; it still calls NewSQLCommand. SQL is currently blocked only incidentally because sql.TablesList now fails when the stub DB returns 'not implemented', producing a misleading 'error reading SQL command' BadRequest. This defense-in-depth gap means restoring or replacing the stub DB implementation would silently re-enable the vulnerable SQL path through this entry point without any explicit feature/security gate. Add the same explicit rejection here (and for direct NewSQLCommand/SQLCommand execution) rather than relying on the stubbed database to fail.

No regression test covers disabling SQL expressions

The PR changes the SQL query path to reject QueryTypeSQL and stubs out the SQL database, but adds or updates no tests. There is no test proving that a SQL expression is rejected even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled, nor tests covering NewSQLCommand/UnmarshalSQLCommand and SQLCommand.Execute failing closed with the stubbed DB. Without these, a future refactor of the reader, command unmarshalling, or DB stub could accidentally re-enable the CVE-2024-9264 attack surface without CI noticing.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key now race and leak/conflict

BuildIndex no longer holds cacheMu while checking/creating/building the index, and only locks briefly to store the finished index at line 137-139. GetIndex therefore returns nil for the whole duration of an in-flight build, so two concurrent Search/getOrCreateIndex calls (or init plus a watch event) for the same NamespacedResource both build an index. For file-backed indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory and can fail with lock/already-exists errors; for memory indexes both do the full scan and the later store silently overwrites and leaks the earlier unclosed bleve index. The old whole-build lock also made concurrent builders serialize. A per-key build lock/singleflight, or double-checked locking around cache insertion, is needed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without taking cacheMu.RLock. With the finer-grained locking in this PR, BuildIndex now inserts into b.cache (line 137-139) while other work is in flight, and searchSupport.init calls TotalDocs after it has already started the watch goroutine that can trigger further builds. Concurrent map iteration and map write in Go can panic with 'concurrent map iteration and map write' and is a data race. TotalDocs must snapshot or iterate the cache under RLock.

false_positives.candidate:
NewResourceServer now blocks on full index build and fails construction on search/watch errors

NewResourceServer now synchronously calls s.Init(ctx), which builds every search index (searchSupport.init scans all namespaces over initMinCount) and starts the watcher before returning. Previously construction was cheap and initialization happened lazily on the first gRPC call, so callers could construct the server and serve non-search endpoints (Read, IsHealthy, blob) even if index building was slow or the watch/stats backend was unavailable. Now a slow or failing GetResourceStats/WatchWriteEvents makes NewResourceServer hang for the whole index build or return an error for the entire server, and the background context used has no timeout, so startup can block indefinitely. This is the lazy-initialization dependency the PR description asks about and should be confirmed against all constructors/callers (including tests using fake backends without watch/stats support), or startup should remain non-blocking with readiness reported separately.

Postgres storage-server integration test is skipped rather than fixed

The PR adds a blanket skip for GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres in TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer, the only integration test exercising the storage-server target end to end. Since this PR changes ResourceServer startup/initialization, losing the postgres run removes coverage for exactly the changed startup path on a supported backend; the stated failure ('not working with postgres in Drone') is left uninvestigated and could hide a real postgres-specific initialization regression introduced here.

init worker goroutines race on totalBatchesIndexed and err

searchSupport.init launches up to initWorkers goroutines via errgroup, and each goroutine does totalBatchesIndexed++ (line 189) and assigns to the shared outer err variable (line 190: '_, _, err = s.build(...)') without synchronization. Concurrent increments can be lost (so the span attribute is wrong) and concurrent writes to err are a data race that go test -race will flag; a failing build's error can also be overwritten by a concurrent successful write before it is returned to errgroup. Use an atomic counter and a goroutine-local err variable returned from the closure.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New test cleanup removes a literal alias instead of the created IdPs

Each loop iteration creates an IdP aliased "idp-alias-" + i but registers cleanup as testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove, using the literal string "alias" rather than the created alias (the same mistake is repeated for idp-alias-20 at line 425). Cleanup therefore does not remove the twenty created providers and may attempt to remove a non-existent provider, leaving state that can pollute subsequent tests using the shared test realm and mask or cause cache-count failures.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation compares an organization-aware original with a raw updated model

update() obtains the original through getById(), which returns createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(): its isEnabled() also returns false when the linked organization is disabled. The updated model passed by callers is normally the raw model. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() therefore evaluates LoginFilter.ENABLED against different semantics for the two models. For example, for an enabled public broker in a disabled organization whose BROKER_PUBLIC is changed from true to false, the wrapped original already fails the login predicate because isEnabled() is false, and the raw updated model also fails it because it is no longer public, so both are treated as 'not a login IdP' and no invalidation is registered. The stale cached getForLogin list can then expose the now-private broker after the organization is re-enabled. The original's underlying IdP fields, not the organization-aware isEnabled(), must be used for this comparison.

New login predicate can NPE on an IdP model with null config

getLoginPredicate() now unconditionally calls idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC) for every organization-linked IdP. IdentityProviderModel.setConfig() allows the config map to be replaced, including with null, and previously this predicate only called simple boolean getters. The Infinispan provider now invokes this predicate from create(), update(), and remove() invalidation handling, so an org-linked model with a null config can fail those operations with a NullPointerException instead of being created, updated, or removed. The predicate should treat a null config as not public.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns an arbitrary non-BouncyCastle provider

The CryptoProvider contract states getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the (FIPS or non-FIPS) BouncyCastle provider, but this implementation returns the provider of the JVM default KeyStore type (typically SUN/SunJSSE for PKCS12). Any caller that uses the returned provider for BC-only algorithms, keystore types or provider-name assumptions will get NoSuchAlgorithm/NoSuchProvider failures or silently different crypto behaviour. Like WildFlyElytronProvider, it should return null if no BC provider exists, or throw UnsupportedOperationException, rather than misidentify an unrelated JCA provider as BouncyCastle.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is a public extension interface, but order() is added as an abstract method. Every existing implementation outside the three updated in this PR (custom server providers, downstream/client-repo implementations, mocks and test doubles) will fail to compile until it adds order(). This is an avoidable source/binary contract break for an ordering feature: order() should be a default method with a documented default priority, with built-in providers overriding it as needed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
ECDSA test never verifies the produced DER signature and does not test provider ordering

test() only checks DER->RS->DER->RS self-consistency using the same custom ASN.1 encoder/decoder pair, and generates a single default EC key pair regardless of whether ES256, ES384 or ES512 is under test. A mutually compensating encoder/decoder defect, or DER that JCA rejects, would still pass, and the central new behaviour of this PR (CryptoIntegration choosing between AuthzClientCryptoProvider order 100 and a full provider order 200, including tie handling) has no test at all. The test should verify asn1Des with Signature.verify() using a curve-appropriate key pair, and CryptoIntegration selection should be covered directly.

Equal-order providers are silently and nondeterministically selected instead of rejected

detectProvider() sorts by order() descending and unconditionally returns the first provider. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so when more than one is on the classpath the winner depends on ServiceLoader encounter/classpath order. Previously this configuration failed fast with 'Multiple crypto providers loaded'; now Keycloak can silently run with DefaultCryptoProvider instead of the FIPS provider (or vice versa), defeating an operator's explicit FIPS configuration and hiding a misconfiguration. Ties for the highest order should remain an error, or the mutually exclusive full providers need distinct, intentional priorities.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
hasPermission can dereference a null all-clients resource

When no resource exists for the specific client, the code loads the all-clients resource via AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource() and immediately passes it to policyStore.findByResource() and later calls resource.getScopes(). getResourceTypeResource() can return null (for example when the Clients all-resource resource is absent, as in realms initialized before this resource type existed). That turns a normal permission check into a NullPointerException/500 instead of returning false, potentially breaking client admin endpoints for the whole realm.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Existing FGAPv2 realms never receive the new Clients resource type or scopes

init() returns immediately whenever realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is non-null. Realms that enabled admin permissions before this change therefore keep only the Users all-resource resource and the old scope set; they never get the Clients all-resource resource or the new configure/map-roles-client-scope/map-roles-composite scopes. Creating a Clients scope permission in such a realm can fail while resolving scopes, and client permission evaluation that falls back to the Clients resource type has no resource to evaluate, so the new feature is broken for upgraded/existing realms rather than only for newly initialized ones.

getResourceName does not translate Clients resources

getResourceName() only special-cases the Users resource type: it returns 'All users' for the all-users resource and resolves a user ID to a username, throwing if the user is missing. Clients resources fall through to resource.getDisplayName(). Resources created by getOrCreateResource() are created with the client ID as the resource name and no display name, and the all-clients resource is named 'Clients'. As a result, permission/resource representations for the new Clients type will expose a null/blank display name (or raw UUID) instead of 'All clients' or the client's clientId, unlike the Users behavior this feature mirrors.

setPermissionsEnabled now throws for callers reached through MgmtPermissionsV2

MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() now always returns ClientPermissionsV2, whose setPermissionsEnabled() and isPermissionsEnabled() throw UnsupportedOperationException. Generic management callers still invoke these methods, notably AdminPermissions.registerListener() on ClientRemovedEvent/RoleRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent via AdminPermissions.management(), which selects MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever the V2 feature is enabled even though the listener only checks the V1 feature flag. If both FGAP features are enabled, deleting a client/role/group can fail with UnsupportedOperationException instead of performing the old cleanup/no-op, and other generic client-permission endpoints that probe isPermissionsEnabled() risk the same 500.

Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
