A regression or a swapped/misreported exit code (consequential because 4 previously meant recreate) would therefore pass the suite while breaking scripts and consumers that follow the documented exit-code contract.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
VIEW-only group permission grants global group manage

canManage() with no group argument returns hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE), so an admin granted only the view scope on all Groups passes requireManage(). That check is used, for example, by GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup to authorize creating top-level groups, so a read-only FGAP admin can create groups. Unlike canManage(GroupModel), which correctly requires only MANAGE, the global check should not treat VIEW as sufficient.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns and looks up authorization resource IDs instead of group IDs

The method passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission(), but hasPermission() treats that argument as a group ID and calls resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId). For resources created by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource, the resource name is the group ID while getId() is the authorization store's generated resource ID, so the lookup misses and falls back to the all-groups resource. It also adds groupResource.getId() to the returned set, whereas callers such as UsersResource.searchForUser and getUsersCount expect real group IDs for the UserModel.GROUPS filter/count. Per-group view-members/manage-members grants can therefore be lost or produce counts/filters that match no group; the resource name (the group ID) should be used in both places.

false_positives.candidate:
getResourceName does not resolve Groups resources

getResourceName() special-cases only the Users resource type: it returns 'All users' and resolves individual user IDs to usernames, but has no corresponding branch for GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE. Group policies therefore fall back to resource.getDisplayName(), which for schema-created group resources is the group ID rather than the group name (and never yields an 'All groups' label), so the admin authorization UI/API shows opaque IDs for the newly added Groups resource type.

hasPermission can NPE when the all-groups resource does not exist

When no specific group resource is found, hasPermission() assigns resource from getResourceTypeResource() and immediately calls policyStore.findByResource(server, resource) without a null check, and later dereferences resource.getScopes(). getResourceTypeResource() returns null when the Groups type resource has not been created (for example before schema initialization completes or after it is removed), so permission checks such as canView()/canManage() can fail with a NullPointerException/500 instead of returning false/Forbidden.

The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

false_positives.candidate:
Anchor pattern matches non-anchor tags and misses uppercase anchors

ANCHOR_PATTERN is '</?a[^>]*>' with no word boundary and no case-insensitivity. It therefore treats tags such as <abbr>, <article> or <address> as anchors and can strip them from the checked value when they happen to match the English string, bypassing the HTML policy for elements that were never intended to be whitelisted. Conversely a legitimate <A HREF=...> anchor identical to the English source is not recognised, is left in the value and is then reported as illegal HTML. The pattern needs a boundary after 'a' (and case-insensitive matching) to represent anchor tags only.

When a translated anchor does not match the English source, santizeAnchors() adds only "Didn't find anchor tag ... in original string". Unlike the Illegal HTML message it omits the message key and the file being verified, so when the plugin checks hundreds of properties files in CI the maintainer cannot locate the offending entry from the build output without re-running or searching manually.

Lithuanian loginTotpStep1 was replaced with Italian text

The Lithuanian login message loginTotpStep1 now reads 'Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:' which is Italian, not Lithuanian. As with the account bundle, removing the FreeOTP/Google Play anchors replaced the Lithuanian translation with the Italian sentence, so the login TOTP instructions will be shown in the wrong language.

verifySafeHtml() derives the English file by regex-replacing the locale and community path in the absolute path, then throws a raw RuntimeException if that file cannot be opened. verify() only translates IOException from reading the target file into MojoExecutionException, so a properties file with no matching _en counterpart (or a path the regex does not rewrite as expected) crashes the whole verifier run with a stack trace instead of producing a per-file verification message or checking the remaining files.

No positive test that legitimate HTML and matching anchors pass All new tests only assert that a violation is reported (illegal tag, HTML where English has none, changed anchor). There is no fixture asserting an empty result for a translation that reuses exactly the English string's allowed HTML (

//
) and identical anchor, nor for the special-case normalisations (choice formats, templateHelp). A regression that flags every HTML-containing translation would still pass the whole suite while breaking the verifier for the real message bundles.

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Constructor validates grantType twice and never validates rawTokenId

Line 72 checks grantType and line 73 checks grantType again with the message 'Null rawTokenId not allowed'; rawTokenId itself is never null-checked. A null rawTokenId therefore passes construction and later produces a token ID ending in ':null' from encodeTokenId(), or corrupt data returned from getRawTokenId(), instead of failing fast at the point of the programming error.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted logic and wrong substring offset

The encoded prefix is session(0-1)+tokenType(2-3)+grant(4-5), but the matcher checks substring(3,5), and returns false when that substring equals the expected grant shortcut instead of when it differs. As written it rejects (partly) matching IDs for the wrong reason and accepts IDs whose grant shortcut is wrong, so expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken do not actually verify the grant-type encoding this PR introduces. It should check substring(4,6) and return false on inequality.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Shortcut length/uniqueness contract is not validated but decoder assumes exactly 2 chars

postInit() registers whatever getShortcut() returns without checking it is non-null and exactly 2 characters, and the interface javadoc even suggests 'usually like 3-letters'. encodeTokenId() simply concatenates the shortcut, so a 1- or 3-character (or null) shortcut produces a token ID whose prefix is not 6 characters (or an NPE from ConcurrentHashMap.put for null), and getTokenContextFromTokenId() will then reject every such token with IllegalArgumentException. The factory only checks duplicate map sizes, not the format the wire encoding depends on.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

false_positives.candidate:
Decoder throws on any colon-containing token ID that is not in the new format

getTokenContextFromTokenId() returns UNKNOWN only when the ID contains no ':' at all; any other ID containing a colon but with a prefix that is not exactly 6 known characters throws IllegalArgumentException. Token IDs are attacker/client-influenced input (jti of presented tokens) and older or externally/custom-generated IDs may legitimately contain colons. Future consumers using this decoder for introspection/userinfo/session lookup (the stated purpose of the PR) will turn such tokens into 500 errors instead of treating the context as unknown like pre-upgrade UUID tokens.

New abstract getShortcut() breaks all custom grant-type factories

getShortcut() was added as an abstract interface method with no default implementation. Every existing custom OAuth2GrantTypeFactory outside this PR (and any test/deployment extension implementing the old interface) will fail to compile, and already-compiled implementations will throw AbstractMethodError when the encoder factory calls getShortcut() during postInit or token issuance. A default method (e.g. returning the unknown shortcut) is needed to preserve SPI compatibility.

Public copy constructor of OAuth2GrantType.Context was removed

The public Context(Context) copy constructor was deleted and replaced by initialization of grantType from formParams. Code that copied a grant context (custom grants, token-exchange flows, tests) no longer compiles. In addition, grantType is now captured once from formParams at construction, so a later setFormParams() call silently leaves getGrantType() returning the stale original value, which is then encoded into the access-token ID.

Token issuance now fails for any unregistered grant type

encodeTokenId() throws IllegalStateException whenever getShortcutByGrantType() returns null, and TokenManager.initToken() now calls this for every access token. Previously token creation never depended on the grant type being known to this registry. Any flow that sets Constants.GRANT_TYPE to a value without a registered OAuth2GrantTypeFactory with that exact ID (custom grants, non-grant issuance paths that propagate a grant string, or a grant whose factory is feature-disabled and absent from the session factory) will now fail token creation entirely instead of issuing a token with an unknown-context ID.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

false_positives.candidate:
Exhausted federated recovery credentials are not removed

When allCodesUsed() is true, the code calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(...). That operation removes credentials from Keycloak's local credential store only; it does not delete or disable a credential owned by a federated user storage. Because getCredential() now preferentially returns the federated credential, an exhausted federated credential can remain configured after this call while a CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is also added, leaving stale/used codes in the external storage and potentially causing repeated setup or inconsistent configuredFor state.

Federated recovery codes are never marked as used and can be replayed

After credentialManager().isValid() succeeds, this code only checks RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.allCodesUsed() on the fetched credential. For a local credential, Keycloak's recovery-code provider consumes the code as part of validation and persists that state; for a federated credential, validation is delegated to the user storage's CredentialInputValidator, which merely validates the input (as the test provider does) and does not update the hashed code list or its used flags. Nothing here calls updateCredential/disableCredentialType to persist consumption. Consequently the same federated recovery code can be reused indefinitely, and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean will keep asking for the first unused code instead of advancing to the next code.

Federated recovery credential loses user label and generation time

The UserCredentialModel sent to user storage is constructed only from credentialModel.getType() and the generated-code JSON. It does not carry credentialModel's userLabel or createdDate/generation time, even though RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(generatedCodes, generatedAtTime, generatedUserLabel) was built with those values in RecoveryAuthnCodesAction. Federated providers therefore cannot persist the label/date chosen at setup; the test provider substitutes the current time and a null label, so account/console displays and credential metadata for federated recovery codes will be wrong or empty.

Federated recovery-code test does not verify single-use or code advancement

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin logs in once with the code at index 0 and logs out. It does not attempt to reuse the same code, log in again with the next code, verify that the login page requests the next code number, or verify behavior when all codes are exhausted. Those are the main behavioral differences between local hashed recovery credentials and federated validation, so the current test would pass even though federated codes remain replayable and never advance.

Raw recovery codes are sent to user storage instead of the hashed credential data

credentialModel already contains the recovery codes in Keycloak's hashed credential representation, but createRecoveryCodesCredential discards that data and sends JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes), i.e. the plaintext codes, as the UserCredentialModel challenge response. A federated provider that persists the challenge response verbatim (the added BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage does exactly that) will store usable recovery codes in plaintext, unlike local storage which stores hashes. Compromise of the federated store would therefore disclose valid recovery codes; the helper should pass the hashed credential data or clearly require/implement hashing in the storage contract.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined, making the regression test racy and leaky

The reader thread is started but never joined. The main thread sets deletedAll at line 155 and immediately asserts caughtExceptions is empty at line 157, while the reader may still be inside groups() and may record an exception only after the assertion, producing false passes. Conversely the unjoined busy-loop thread can outlive the test and keep calling managedRealm.admin() during/after test teardown, interfering with subsequent tests. If the cached group is deleted concurrently and the delegate lookup therefore returns null, these methods throw the same NullPointerException the PR is intended to eliminate, e.g. when listing/searching subgroups of a group being deleted.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hung spawn flusher is never killed before being replaced

Flusher workers are created with multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, whose objects are SpawnProcess/BaseProcess instances, not instances of multiprocessing.Process. The isinstance check therefore never passes in production, so a worker detected as hung is not killed before _create_process_for_shards starts its replacement. The hung worker can keep polling and flushing the same Redis shards concurrently with the new worker, causing duplicate buffered-segment production and races between flush_segments/done_flush_segments, while the reference to the leaked worker is overwritten in self.processes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: flusher processes are created using `multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process` (resulting in `SpawnProcess` instances), which causes the `isinstance(..., multiprocessing.Process)` check to fail and prevents hung processes from being killed.

false_positives.candidate:
join() never terminates spawn flusher processes

For the same reason as the restart path, isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is false for processes created through the spawn context (and for the threading.Thread workers used when produce_to_pipe is set, terminate is inapplicable). After join() waits until its deadline for workers that ignore the shared stopped flag, the terminate call is skipped, so shutdown can return while daemon flusher processes are still alive flushing segments and producing to Kafka; they are only cleaned up implicitly when the parent process exits.

The CLI option added for process-spans accepts any integer and SpanFlusher performs no positive-value validation. Passing 0 is silently changed by `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` into one process per shard, the opposite of an operator's explicit request, while a negative value makes num_processes negative, builds an empty process_to_shards_map, and then fails with a KeyError on `i % self.num_processes` during shard assignment instead of a clear configuration error at startup.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
VIEW-only group permission grants global group manage

canManage() with no group argument returns hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE), so an admin granted only the view scope on all Groups passes requireManage(). That check is used, for example, by GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup to authorize creating top-level groups, so a read-only FGAP admin can create groups. Unlike canManage(GroupModel), which correctly requires only MANAGE, the global check should not treat VIEW as sufficient.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: the `canManage()` method erroneously includes `AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW` in its `hasPermission` check, which allows users with only VIEW permission to pass the manage check.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns and looks up authorization resource IDs instead of group IDs

The method passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission(), but hasPermission() treats that argument as a group ID and calls resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId). For resources created by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource, the resource name is the group ID while getId() is the authorization store's generated resource ID, so the lookup misses and falls back to the all-groups resource. It also adds groupResource.getId() to the returned set, whereas callers such as UsersResource.searchForUser and getUsersCount expect real group IDs for the UserModel.GROUPS filter/count. Per-group view-members/manage-members grants can therefore be lost or produce counts/filters that match no group; the resource name (the group ID) should be used in both places.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission` uses `groupResource.getId()` (the authorization resource ID) instead of the resource name (the actual group ID) when calling `hasPermission` and populating the returned set, causing lookups to fail/fall back to 'all-groups' and returning invalid group IDs for downstream user queries/counts.

false_positives.candidate:
hasPermission can NPE when the all-groups resource does not exist

When no specific group resource is found, hasPermission() assigns resource from getResourceTypeResource() and immediately calls policyStore.findByResource(server, resource) without a null check, and later dereferences resource.getScopes(). getResourceTypeResource() returns null when the Groups type resource has not been created (for example before schema initialization completes or after it is removed), so permission checks such as canView()/canManage() can fail with a NullPointerException/500 instead of returning false/Forbidden.

getResourceName does not resolve Groups resources

getResourceName() special-cases only the Users resource type: it returns 'All users' and resolves individual user IDs to usernames, but has no corresponding branch for GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE. Group policies therefore fall back to resource.getDisplayName(), which for schema-created group resources is the group ID rather than the group name (and never yields an 'All groups' label), so the admin authorization UI/API shows opaque IDs for the newly added Groups resource type.

false_positives.candidate:
Missing English bundle aborts verification with an unhandled RuntimeException

verifySafeHtml() derives the English file by regex-replacing the locale and community path in the absolute path, then throws a raw RuntimeException if that file cannot be opened. verify() only translates IOException from reading the target file into MojoExecutionException, so a properties file with no matching _en counterpart (or a path the regex does not rewrite as expected) crashes the whole verifier run with a stack trace instead of producing a per-file verification message or checking the remaining files.

Anchor pattern matches non-anchor tags and misses uppercase anchors

ANCHOR_PATTERN is '</?a[^>]*>' with no word boundary and no case-insensitivity. It therefore treats tags such as <abbr>, <article> or <address> as anchors and can strip them from the checked value when they happen to match the English string, bypassing the HTML policy for elements that were never intended to be whitelisted. Conversely a legitimate <A HREF=...> anchor identical to the English source is not recognised, is left in the value and is then reported as illegal HTML. The pattern needs a boundary after 'a' (and case-insensitive matching) to represent anchor tags only.

Anchor-mismatch message identifies neither the key nor the file

When a translated anchor does not match the English source, santizeAnchors() adds only "Didn't find anchor tag ... in original string". Unlike the Illegal HTML message it omits the message key and the file being verified, so when the plugin checks hundreds of properties files in CI the maintainer cannot locate the offending entry from the build output without re-running or searching manually.

Lithuanian loginTotpStep1 was replaced with Italian text

As with the account bundle, removing the FreeOTP/Google Play anchors replaced the Lithuanian translation with the Italian sentence, so the login TOTP instructions will be shown in the wrong language.

//

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.

isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted logic and wrong substring offset

As written it rejects (partly) matching IDs for the wrong reason and accepts IDs whose grant shortcut is wrong, so expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken do not actually verify the grant-type encoding this PR introduces. true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Shortcut length/uniqueness contract is not validated but decoder assumes exactly 2 chars

postInit() registers whatever getShortcut() returns without checking it is non-null and exactly 2 characters, and the interface javadoc even suggests 'usually like 3-letters'. encodeTokenId() simply concatenates the shortcut, so a 1- or 3-character (or null) shortcut produces a token ID whose prefix is not 6 characters (or an NPE from ConcurrentHashMap.put for null), and getTokenContextFromTokenId() will then reject every such token with IllegalArgumentException. The factory only checks duplicate map sizes, not the format the wire encoding depends on.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue point out the discrepancy between the interface Javadoc (which suggests 'usually like 3-letters' for shortcuts) and the actual implementation/usage which relies on 2-character shortcuts. The candidate expands on why this is problematic in the decoder, while the golden comment simply suggests updating the documentation, but they identify the exact same underlying inconsistency.

false_positives.candidate:
New abstract getShortcut() breaks all custom grant-type factories

getShortcut() was added as an abstract interface method with no default implementation. Every existing custom OAuth2GrantTypeFactory outside this PR (and any test/deployment extension implementing the old interface) will fail to compile, and already-compiled implementations will throw AbstractMethodError when the encoder factory calls getShortcut() during postInit or token issuance. A default method (e.g. returning the unknown shortcut) is needed to preserve SPI compatibility.

Public copy constructor of OAuth2GrantType.Context was removed

The public Context(Context) copy constructor was deleted and replaced by initialization of grantType from formParams. Code that copied a grant context (custom grants, token-exchange flows, tests) no longer compiles. In addition, grantType is now captured once from formParams at construction, so a later setFormParams() call silently leaves getGrantType() returning the stale original value, which is then encoded into the access-token ID.

Token issuance now fails for any unregistered grant type

encodeTokenId() throws IllegalStateException whenever getShortcutByGrantType() returns null, and TokenManager.initToken() now calls this for every access token. Previously token creation never depended on the grant type being known to this registry. Any flow that sets Constants.GRANT_TYPE to a value without a registered OAuth2GrantTypeFactory with that exact ID (custom grants, non-grant issuance paths that propagate a grant string, or a grant whose factory is feature-disabled and absent from the session factory) will now fail token creation entirely instead of issuing a token with an unknown-context ID.

Decoder throws on any colon-containing token ID that is not in the new format

getTokenContextFromTokenId() returns UNKNOWN only when the ID contains no ':' at all; any other ID containing a colon but with a prefix that is not exactly 6 known characters throws IllegalArgumentException. Token IDs are attacker/client-influenced input (jti of presented tokens) and older or externally/custom-generated IDs may legitimately contain colons. Future consumers using this decoder for introspection/userinfo/session lookup (the stated purpose of the PR) will turn such tokens into 500 errors instead of treating the context as unknown like pre-upgrade UUID tokens.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

false_positives.candidate:
Federated recovery codes are never marked as used and can be replayed

After credentialManager().isValid() succeeds, this code only checks RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.allCodesUsed() on the fetched credential. For a local credential, Keycloak's recovery-code provider consumes the code as part of validation and persists that state; for a federated credential, validation is delegated to the user storage's CredentialInputValidator, which merely validates the input (as the test provider does) and does not update the hashed code list or its used flags. Nothing here calls updateCredential/disableCredentialType to persist consumption. Consequently the same federated recovery code can be reused indefinitely, and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean will keep asking for the first unused code instead of advancing to the next code.

Exhausted federated recovery credentials are not removed

When allCodesUsed() is true, the code calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(...). That operation removes credentials from Keycloak's local credential store only; it does not delete or disable a credential owned by a federated user storage. Because getCredential() now preferentially returns the federated credential, an exhausted federated credential can remain configured after this call while a CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is also added, leaving stale/used codes in the external storage and potentially causing repeated setup or inconsistent configuredFor state.

Raw recovery codes are sent to user storage instead of the hashed credential data

credentialModel already contains the recovery codes in Keycloak's hashed credential representation, but createRecoveryCodesCredential discards that data and sends JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes), i.e. the plaintext codes, as the UserCredentialModel challenge response. A federated provider that persists the challenge response verbatim (the added BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage does exactly that) will store usable recovery codes in plaintext, unlike local storage which stores hashes. Compromise of the federated store would therefore disclose valid recovery codes; the helper should pass the hashed credential data or clearly require/implement hashing in the storage contract.

Federated recovery credential loses user label and generation time

The UserCredentialModel sent to user storage is constructed only from credentialModel.getType() and the generated-code JSON. It does not carry credentialModel's userLabel or createdDate/generation time, even though RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(generatedCodes, generatedAtTime, generatedUserLabel) was built with those values in RecoveryAuthnCodesAction. Federated providers therefore cannot persist the label/date chosen at setup; the test provider substitutes the current time and a null label, so account/console displays and credential metadata for federated recovery codes will be wrong or empty.

Federated recovery-code test does not verify single-use or code advancement

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin logs in once with the code at index 0 and logs out. It does not attempt to reuse the same code, log in again with the next code, verify that the login page requests the next code number, or verify behavior when all codes are exhausted. Those are the main behavioral differences between local hashed recovery credentials and federated validation, so the current test would pass even though federated codes remain replayable and never advance.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

New and changed CLI exit codes are not asserted by tests

A regression or a swapped/misreported exit code (consequential because 4 previously meant recreate) would therefore pass the suite while breaking scripts and consumers that follow the documented exit-code contract.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
hasPermission can dereference a null all-clients resource

When no resource exists for the specific client, the code loads the all-clients resource via AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource() and immediately passes it to policyStore.findByResource() and later calls resource.getScopes(). getResourceTypeResource() can return null (for example when the Clients all-resource resource is absent, as in realms initialized before this resource type existed). false_positives.candidate:
Existing FGAPv2 realms never receive the new Clients resource type or scopes

init() returns immediately whenever realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is non-null. Realms that enabled admin permissions before this change therefore keep only the Users all-resource resource and the old scope set; they never get the Clients all-resource resource or the new configure/map-roles-client-scope/map-roles-composite scopes. Creating a Clients scope permission in such a realm can fail while resolving scopes, and client permission evaluation that falls back to the Clients resource type has no resource to evaluate, so the new feature is broken for upgraded/existing realms rather than only for newly initialized ones.

setPermissionsEnabled now throws for callers reached through MgmtPermissionsV2

MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() now always returns ClientPermissionsV2, whose setPermissionsEnabled() and isPermissionsEnabled() throw UnsupportedOperationException. If both FGAP features are enabled, deleting a client/role/group can fail with UnsupportedOperationException instead of performing the old cleanup/no-op, and other generic client-permission endpoints that probe isPermissionsEnabled() risk the same 500.

getResourceName does not translate Clients resources

getResourceName() only special-cases the Users resource type: it returns 'All users' for the all-users resource and resolves a user ID to a username, throwing if the user is missing. Clients resources fall through to resource.getDisplayName(). Resources created by getOrCreateResource() are created with the client ID as the resource name and no display name, and the all-clients resource is named 'Clients'. As a result, permission/resource representations for the new Clients type will expose a null/blank display name (or raw UUID) instead of 'All clients' or the client's clientId, unlike the Users behavior this feature mirrors.

Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns an arbitrary non-BouncyCastle provider

The CryptoProvider contract states getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the (FIPS or non-FIPS) BouncyCastle provider, but this implementation returns the provider of the JVM default KeyStore type (typically SUN/SunJSSE for PKCS12). Any caller that uses the returned provider for BC-only algorithms, keystore types or provider-name assumptions will get NoSuchAlgorithm/NoSuchProvider failures or silently different crypto behaviour. Like WildFlyElytronProvider, it should return null if no BC provider exists, or throw UnsupportedOperationException, rather than misidentify an unrelated JCA provider as BouncyCastle.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is a public extension interface, but order() is added as an abstract method. Every existing implementation outside the three updated in this PR (custom server providers, downstream/client-repo implementations, mocks and test doubles) will fail to compile until it adds order(). This is an avoidable source/binary contract break for an ordering feature: order() should be a default method with a documented default priority, with built-in providers overriding it as needed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same problem: adding an abstract `order()` method to the `CryptoProvider` interface will break backward compatibility for existing implementations.

false_positives.candidate:
Equal-order providers are silently and nondeterministically selected instead of rejected

detectProvider() sorts by order() descending and unconditionally returns the first provider. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so when more than one is on the classpath the winner depends on ServiceLoader encounter/classpath order. Previously this configuration failed fast with 'Multiple crypto providers loaded'; now Keycloak can silently run with DefaultCryptoProvider instead of the FIPS provider (or vice versa), defeating an operator's explicit FIPS configuration and hiding a misconfiguration. Ties for the highest order should remain an error, or the mutually exclusive full providers need distinct, intentional priorities.

ECDSA test never verifies the produced DER signature and does not test provider ordering

test() only checks DER->RS->DER->RS self-consistency using the same custom ASN.1 encoder/decoder pair, and generates a single default EC key pair regardless of whether ES256, ES384 or ES512 is under test. A mutually compensating encoder/decoder defect, or DER that JCA rejects, would still pass, and the central new behaviour of this PR (CryptoIntegration choosing between AuthzClientCryptoProvider order 100 and a full provider order 200, including tie handling) has no test at all. The test should verify asn1Des with Signature.verify() using a curve-appropriate key pair, and CryptoIntegration selection should be covered directly.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.

true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue point out the exact same bug: `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` requiring `user != null` causes `authenticate(...)` not to call `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` on the initial login page where `context.getUser()` is null, thereby breaking conditional passkey UI for initial passwordless login.

false_positives.candidate:
Re-authentication skip is disabled for all users when realm passkeys are enabled, even users with no passkey

Assuming the intended check is the realm-level isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()), it only tests that passkeys are enabled for the realm and a user is present; it never checks that this user actually has a passwordless WebAuthn credential. Consequently, during re-authentication (e.g. prompt=login) in the split UsernameForm+PasswordForm flow, users who previously were silently skipped through UsernameForm because they have no linked IdP will now always be stopped at the username form, even though they cannot use a passkey and must manually submit the (hidden-username) form to reach the password step. This is a behaviour regression for non-passkey users in passkey-enabled realms; the skip should only be suppressed when the current user could actually authenticate with a passkey.

false_positives.candidate:
Queues are unbounded despite claimed backpressure

FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with the default maxsize=0 (unbounded), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() never blocks or rejects. The docstring at lines 253-254 promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but under a slow result_processor the Arroyo processor will keep submitting messages indefinitely, growing memory without bound and building a huge outstanding-offset set (also delaying commits past max.poll.interval). Bound the queues and make submit() apply backpressure, or remove the claim and add another flow-control mechanism.

Shutdown abandons queued-but-unprocessed items

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True for every worker before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker.run() re-checks `while not self.shutdown` after each item, so a worker that finishes its current item exits even if its queue still holds pending items (which immediate=False was supposed to drain). Those items are never processed and their offsets stay outstanding forever in this process; graceful shutdown silently drops in-flight work (only redelivery on restart saves it, and only if offsets were not already marked complete). Don't set the flag until queues are drained, or have workers exit only when the queue is empty and shut down.

close() stops the commit loop before workers drain

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread first, and only then calls queue_pool.shutdown(). Any items the workers finish during pool shutdown therefore complete their offsets after the last _commit_loop iteration, so those offsets are never passed to commit_function. Arroyo will consider the strategy closed and will not poll again, so successfully processed messages are redelivered and reprocessed on restart. Drain the pool first (and run a final commit pass), then stop the commit thread.

Queue pool is created once in the factory but killed by each strategy close

FixedQueuePool is constructed a single time in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ (line 133) and the same instance is handed to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy from create_with_partitions(). Arroyo calls create_with_partitions() again after a rebalance/revocation, but the previous strategy's close()/terminate() calls queue_pool.shutdown(), which shuts down the shared queues and joins the workers. The next strategy reuses that dead pool: work_queue.put() raises queue.ShutDown, which SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() catches and converts into add_offset+complete_offset, so messages are silently dropped yet committed. Create a fresh pool per create_with_partitions() call (or make the pool restartable and don't shut it down in strategy close).

submit() marks messages complete and committable on any error

The bare `except Exception` in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() logs and then does add_offset()+complete_offset() for the message regardless of where the failure occurred - e.g. grouping_fn raising, or FixedQueuePool.submit() failing after add_offset() when putting onto a shut-down queue. Combined with OrderedQueueWorker.run() completing offsets in its `finally` block even when result_processor raises (line 148-149), this contradicts the documented 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and turns transient/poison failures into committed, never-retried message loss instead of letting Arroyo/DLQ handle them. Only skip-and-commit for explicitly undecodable/filtered payloads; propagate or leave outstanding other failures.

Kafka commit function is invoked from a background thread

_commit_loop runs on a dedicated daemon thread and calls self.commit_function(committable) (which is Arroyo's Commit callable built in create_thread_queue_parallel_worker) concurrently with the StreamProcessor main thread that owns submit()/poll()/close(). Arroyo commit callbacks are expected to be invoked from the processing thread during submit/poll/join; racing them against processor-driven commits and shutdown can corrupt/interleave offset state and commit offsets for partitions that have since been revoked. Perform commits from poll() on the strategy thread, using the tracker only to compute committable offsets.

Committable-offset scan is O(range) every second per partition

get_committable_offsets() runs min()/max() over the full all_offsets set and then iterates range(start, max_offset+1) with set lookups, and mark_committed() rebuilds the whole set - all repeated every 1s by _commit_loop for every partition. With a backlog (made likely by the unbounded queues), a single slow offset pins a large outstanding set, so each tick rescans an ever-growing range, giving quadratic behaviour and burning a thread. Track the next-expected offset and a completed set per partition instead of rescanning the whole window.

hash() is not a stable consistent hash for group assignment

get_queue_for_group() uses Python's builtin hash(group_key) % num_queues and documents it as 'consistent hashing'. For str keys hash() is randomised per process via PYTHONHASHSEED, so the group->queue mapping changes on every restart and differs between concurrently running consumer processes; it is also a plain modulo, so changing num_queues (--max-workers) remaps nearly every group. This defeats any cross-restart/cross-process affinity expectations and makes queue distribution non-reproducible in tests/operations. Use a stable digest (e.g. hashlib.md5/sha1 of the key) modulo num_queues.

wait_until_empty reports empty while items are still being processed

wait_until_empty() (and poll()'s total_queued gauge) rely on queue.qsize(), but OrderedQueueWorker removes an item from the queue via get() before it starts processing it. The method therefore returns True while the last item(s) - one per queue - are still in-flight and their offsets not yet completed, so any caller using it as a drain/flush barrier (as shutdown-style tests do) can proceed/commit/tear down too early. Track in-flight counts (e.g. queue.task_done()/join() or an explicit counter incremented on submit and decremented in the worker's finally).

false_positives.candidate:
Switching span sets from SET to ZSET breaks in-flight segments with WRONGTYPE errors

This changes the on-Redis type of span-buf:s:* keys from a Redis SET (sadd/sscan/scard/sunionstore) to a ZSET (zadd/zscan/zcard/zunionstore in buffer.py and add-buffer.lua) with no key versioning, draining, or dual-type handling. During a rolling deploy, keys created by old consumers are SETs; new code calling ZADD/ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZSCAN on them returns WRONGTYPE, failing process_spans/flush for those traces, and old consumers similarly fail on new ZSET keys during rollback. Buffered keys live up to redis_ttl (3600s), so in-flight segments will error and can be dropped for up to an hour around deploys.

Insert-time eviction can silently drop the segment/root span and leaves has_root_span stale

When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, zpopmin evicts the lowest-scored (earliest end_timestamp_precise) members with no metric or log, silently discarding real span payloads rather than flagging the oversized segment as the previous flush-time check did. The evicted members can include the segment/root span (e.g. a short root span, clock skew, or a root whose children report later precise end times); the has_root_span flag computed just below still returns true because it is based on the stored flag or is_root_span of the current insert, so the now root-less segment is queued with the short root timeout and flushed as an incomplete segment. Buffer.py also removed the max_segment_spans guard in _load_segment_data (line 449), so there is no longer any flush-side detection of oversized segments produced by pre-change keys or any path that bypasses this eviction.

No test covers the new eviction, score-ordering, or paginator behavior

The test changes only add the now-required end_timestamp_precise field to existing Span constructions. Nothing exercises a segment growing past 1000 spans to verify zpopmin eviction keeps the intended (latest/root) spans, nothing verifies segments are ordered or deduplicated correctly after the SET-to-ZSET migration, and there are no tests at all for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the optimized_pagination branch in the audit-log endpoint, which currently crash on datetime keys and negative offsets. upsampled_count undercounts events without sample_weight

upsampled_count computes toInt64(sum(sample_weight)) with no coalesce/fallback to 1 for rows where sample_weight is NULL. Allowlisted projects can contain events predating client error sampling, events from SDKs that do not send error_sampling context, or otherwise unsampled events; for those rows sum() ignores NULLs, so a bucket containing only such events returns NULL/0 instead of its real count and mixed buckets silently undercount. The transform in error_upsampling.py applies this to every count() for allowlisted projects, so historical/normal error events disappear from charts. Use a per-row fallback such as coalesce(sample_weight, 1) before summing.

Negated or quoted event.type:error incorrectly triggers upsampling

A query such as '!event.type:error' (explicitly excluding errors, e.g. transaction/default events) contains that substring and returns True, as would the text inside a quoted title/message value. The endpoint then rewrites count() to sum(sample_weight), which does not exist/apply for those non-error events, producing wrong (likely zero/NULL) counts. The query needs to be parsed (or at minimum negation/quoting handled) rather than substring-matched, and spaced forms like 'event.type: error' are also missed by the current check.

Combined with hash() collisions between different project sets for the same organization, one set can also inherit another set's cached eligibility. true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

If cached permissions do not allow the request, Check always calls getIdentityPermissions, which reloads identifiers/basic role/teams (subject to their caches) and queries the permission store and rewrites permCache. The denial cache only helps exact repeats of the same action/name/parent; probing or legitimately checking many distinct resources a user cannot access bypasses it and amplifies each check into a DB query. This removes the negative-case protection previously provided by permCache and creates an easy DB load path via enumeration of resource UIDs.

While the golden comment frames the inconsistency as a security risk (trusting stale grants) and the candidate frames it as a performance/DoS risk (amplifying DB queries on denials), they are pointing to the exact same flawed cache logic in the Check operation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous underscore-concatenation of variable fields

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, userUID, action, name and parent with '_' separators and no escaping or length encoding. Distinct tuples can produce the same key, e.g. name='a_b', parent='c' versus name='a', parent='b_c' (UIDs may contain underscores). A denial recorded for one dashboard/folder can therefore incorrectly deny a different resource for the denial TTL.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same issue: `userPermDenialCacheKey` constructs cache keys by concatenating fields with underscores, leading to potential key collisions and incorrect permission denial cache hits when fields contain underscores.

false_positives.candidate:
Stale denial cache takes precedence over fresher permission cache

Check returns a cached denial before consulting permCache, and no code invalidates permDenialCache when fresh permissions are loaded (for example by List calling getIdentityPermissions and repopulating permCache). If a user is denied, is then granted access, and any path refreshes permCache with the new grant, Check for the same namespace/user/action/name/parent still returns Allowed:false until the denial TTL expires. This can make List show a resource while Check denies it and reintroduces up to 30s of stale denial for permission grants.

Denials caused by a stale folder tree are cached as authoritative denials

When the fresh-permission check fails, Check unconditionally writes permDenialCache. checkPermission/checkInheritedPermissions can fail solely because buildFolderTree returned the 30s-cached folder tree that does not yet contain a newly created or moved parent folder. Such a transient, infrastructure-staleness denial is then stored under the denial key and short-circuits later checks even after the folder tree and permissions have refreshed, extending incorrect denial and undermining the stated goal of letting creators access newly created folders/dashboards promptly in inherited-permission cases.

Because the client-side cache was removed in this PR, callers will reach this server List more often but can still omit newly accessible resources for the full shortCacheTTL (30s). The PR goal of fetching newly created dashboards/folders therefore remains broken for list/fetch flows that rely on List rather than a single Check.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the cancelled request context

Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection all launch `go func()` blocks that derive their timeout with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` from the incoming request context. The Kubernetes request context is cancelled as soon as the handler returns the storage result, which happens immediately after spawning the goroutine, so the legacy write will almost always run with an already-cancelled context and fail/abandon. A detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) before adding the timeout) is required, otherwise mode 3 silently does not perform the legacy writes it exists to perform as a safety net.

Independent goroutines give no ordering for legacy writes

Every write spawns an unsynchronised goroutine for the legacy store. A Create goroutine, a subsequent Update goroutine and a Delete goroutine for the same object can be scheduled or complete out of order (legacy latency is variable up to the 10s timeout): an update can run before the create it depends on and fail as not-found, or a delayed create can run after a delete and resurrect a deleted object in legacy storage. Mode 3 therefore can leave legacy permanently diverged from unified storage; legacy writes need to be serialised/queued per resource or otherwise ordered.

Async legacy calls race on objects shared with the returned response

Create passes the same `obj` pointer to Storage.Create and then to the background Legacy.Create while returning `created` to the caller, and Update passes the same `objInfo` (line 139) to both Storage.Update and the background Legacy.Update. The API server may serialise/mutate the returned object, and UpdatedObjectInfo.UpdatedObject may be invoked a second time against a different old object, concurrently with the first call and with response handling. This is a data race and can make the legacy copy differ from the object written to unified storage; the legacy goroutine needs its own deep copy / the precomputed updated object (as the previous updateWrapper approach provided).

Legacy write failures are never logged

The background goroutines in Create, Delete (line 112), Update (line 139) and DeleteCollection (line 165) discard the legacy error except for a duration metric; the previous synchronous implementation logged these errors. Combined with the fire-and-forget design, an operator has no log signal (with kind/name) that legacy has diverged from unified storage and no way to know which objects need reconciliation. The error branch should log via the request-scoped logger before recording the metric.

Mode 3 tests never verify the async legacy write happens

The Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection tests register legacy mock expectations but return and assert on the storage result immediately, without waiting for the spawned goroutine or calling AssertExpectations/AssertCalled on the legacy mock (both mocks also share a single testify mock.Mock, so expectations cannot even distinguish the two stores). The tests pass even if the legacy write is removed entirely, and if the goroutine fires after the test finishes it can race with later tests using the shared mock and shared example objects. Tests need a synchronisation point (channel/WaitGroup in the mock or Eventually-style assertion) proving legacy is invoked with the right arguments.

New mode 3 integration cases are flaky because legacy visibility is now asynchronous

The added 'mode 3' subtests reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates/updates/deletes via the k8s API and then immediately asserts the objects are visible (and later gone) through the legacy /api/playlists endpoints. In mode 3 the legacy write is performed by a fire-and-forget goroutine started before the response returns, so there is no guarantee it has completed when the very next legacy request is made. These subtests will intermittently fail (missing/extra/stale playlists) unless the legacy assertions poll/wait for eventual consistency.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are not loaded before cached translation lookup

`translate` only loads `config.locale`, not the fallback locales configured in `FallbackLocaleList`. Outside `ApplicationController#set_locale` (background jobs, mailers, console, or translations before that filter) a key missing from the current locale will be looked up in fallback locales whose YAML files have never been loaded via the lazy-loading patch, so it returns a missing-translation string. Worse, the no-argument path stores that result in the LRU cache (`@cache.getset(k) { translate_no_cache(key).freeze }`), so the missing string stays cached under `key+locale` even after the fallback locale is later loaded, until eviction/reload. Fallbacks must be ensured-loaded inside `translate` (or the backend lookup) before computing/caching the value, and the cache must not persist results computed before fallback locales were loaded.

Fallback loading is only wired into web requests

The PR is described as server-side localization fallbacks, but `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is only invoked from `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Server-side code that sets `I18n.locale` and translates without going through this controller (Sidekiq jobs, mailers, rake tasks, plugin background work) never loads the site-default/English fallback files, so with the lazy translation loader those fallbacks silently return missing translations there. The ensure-loaded step belongs in the shared translation path (e.g. `I18n.translate`/`load_locale` logic), not solely in a controller filter.

Fallback lookup queries SiteSetting on every translation

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` is called by the I18n fallbacks backend on every translation lookup, and it calls `SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym` each time. That puts a site-setting lookup (backed by Discourse's setting provider/cache machinery) on the hottest possible path — the very path `translate_accelerator.rb` exists to optimize — and it also raises `NoMethodError` if `default_locale` is ever nil/blank (e.g. early boot or a cleared setting). The fallback chain should be computed without a per-lookup setting query, or at minimum memoized/guarded with a safe default such as `:en`.

No tests cover the custom fallback chain or its lazy loading

This PR introduces a custom `FallbackLocaleList`, replaces the Rails `config.i18n.fallbacks` mechanism, removes the standalone pluralization initializer, and adds `I18n.ensure_loaded!`, but adds no specs. There is nothing verifying that a key missing in the user locale falls back to the site default and then English, that fallback locale files actually get loaded under the lazy-loading patch (including outside controllers), or that pluralized fallback strings still work. Regressions in this global I18n behavior would only surface as missing-translation strings in production; add specs for the fallback order, loading, and a pluralized fallback lookup before merging.

Federated recovery codes are never marked as used and can be replayed

After credentialManager().isValid() succeeds, this code only checks RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.allCodesUsed() on the fetched credential. For a local credential, Keycloak's recovery-code provider consumes the code as part of validation and persists that state; for a federated credential, validation is delegated to the user storage's CredentialInputValidator, which merely validates the input (as the test provider does) and does not update the hashed code list or its used flags. Nothing here calls updateCredential/disableCredentialType to persist consumption. Consequently the same federated recovery code can be reused indefinitely, and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean will keep asking for the first unused code instead of advancing to the next code.

When allCodesUsed() is true, the code calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(...). A federated provider that persists the challenge response verbatim (the added BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage does exactly that) will store usable recovery codes in plaintext, unlike local storage which stores hashes. Compromise of the federated store would therefore disclose valid recovery codes; the helper should pass the hashed credential data or clearly require/implement hashing in the storage contract.

false_positives.candidate:
Queues are unbounded despite claimed backpressure

FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with the default maxsize=0 (unbounded), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() never blocks or rejects. The docstring at lines 253-254 promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but under a slow result_processor the Arroyo processor will keep submitting messages indefinitely, growing memory without bound and building a huge outstanding-offset set (also delaying commits past max.poll.interval). Bound the queues and make submit() apply backpressure, or remove the claim and add another flow-control mechanism.

Shutdown abandons queued-but-unprocessed items

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True for every worker before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker.run() re-checks `while not self.shutdown` after each item, so a worker that finishes its current item exits even if its queue still holds pending items (which immediate=False was supposed to drain). Those items are never processed and their offsets stay outstanding forever in this process; graceful shutdown silently drops in-flight work (only redelivery on restart saves it, and only if offsets were not already marked complete). Don't set the flag until queues are drained, or have workers exit only when the queue is empty and shut down.

close() stops the commit loop before workers drain

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread first, and only then calls queue_pool.shutdown(). Any items the workers finish during pool shutdown therefore complete their offsets after the last _commit_loop iteration, so those offsets are never passed to commit_function. Arroyo will consider the strategy closed and will not poll again, so successfully processed messages are redelivered and reprocessed on restart. Drain the pool first (and run a final commit pass), then stop the commit thread.

Queue pool is created once in the factory but killed by each strategy close

FixedQueuePool is constructed a single time in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ (line 133) and the same instance is handed to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy from create_with_partitions(). Arroyo calls create_with_partitions() again after a rebalance/revocation, but the previous strategy's close()/terminate() calls queue_pool.shutdown(), which shuts down the shared queues and joins the workers. The next strategy reuses that dead pool: work_queue.put() raises queue.ShutDown, which SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() catches and converts into add_offset+complete_offset, so messages are silently dropped yet committed. Create a fresh pool per create_with_partitions() call (or make the pool restartable and don't shut it down in strategy close).

submit() marks messages complete and committable on any error

The bare `except Exception` in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() logs and then does add_offset()+complete_offset() for the message regardless of where the failure occurred - e.g. grouping_fn raising, or FixedQueuePool.submit() failing after add_offset() when putting onto a shut-down queue. Combined with OrderedQueueWorker.run() completing offsets in its `finally` block even when result_processor raises (line 148-149), this contradicts the documented 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and turns transient/poison failures into committed, never-retried message loss instead of letting Arroyo/DLQ handle them. Only skip-and-commit for explicitly undecodable/filtered payloads; propagate or leave outstanding other failures.

Kafka commit function is invoked from a background thread

_commit_loop runs on a dedicated daemon thread and calls self.commit_function(committable) (which is Arroyo's Commit callable built in create_thread_queue_parallel_worker) concurrently with the StreamProcessor main thread that owns submit()/poll()/close(). Arroyo commit callbacks are expected to be invoked from the processing thread during submit/poll/join; racing them against processor-driven commits and shutdown can corrupt/interleave offset state and commit offsets for partitions that have since been revoked. Perform commits from poll() on the strategy thread, using the tracker only to compute committable offsets.

Committable-offset scan is O(range) every second per partition

get_committable_offsets() runs min()/max() over the full all_offsets set and then iterates range(start, max_offset+1) with set lookups, and mark_committed() rebuilds the whole set - all repeated every 1s by _commit_loop for every partition. With a backlog (made likely by the unbounded queues), a single slow offset pins a large outstanding set, so each tick rescans an ever-growing range, giving quadratic behaviour and burning a thread. Track the next-expected offset and a completed set per partition instead of rescanning the whole window.

hash() is not a stable consistent hash for group assignment

get_queue_for_group() uses Python's builtin hash(group_key) % num_queues and documents it as 'consistent hashing'. For str keys hash() is randomised per process via PYTHONHASHSEED, so the group->queue mapping changes on every restart and differs between concurrently running consumer processes; it is also a plain modulo, so changing num_queues (--max-workers) remaps nearly every group. This defeats any cross-restart/cross-process affinity expectations and makes queue distribution non-reproducible in tests/operations. Use a stable digest (e.g. hashlib.md5/sha1 of the key) modulo num_queues.

wait_until_empty reports empty while items are still being processed

wait_until_empty() (and poll()'s total_queued gauge) rely on queue.qsize(), but OrderedQueueWorker removes an item from the queue via get() before it starts processing it. The method therefore returns True while the last item(s) - one per queue - are still in-flight and their offsets not yet completed, so any caller using it as a drain/flush barrier (as shutdown-style tests do) can proceed/commit/tear down too early. Track in-flight counts (e.g. queue.task_done()/join() or an explicit counter incremented on submit and decremented in the worker's finally).

organization_context.member can be None for superusers without org membership

The new gate dereferences organization_context.member.has_global_access unconditionally whenever the optimized path is evaluated (for every request, since enable_advanced is computed before the branch). For a superuser accessing an organization they are not a member of, member can be None, so this raises AttributeError and breaks the previously working audit-log endpoint for exactly the superuser case the check tries to allow (the 'or' short-circuit only helps when is_superuser is already true; a non-superuser request still evaluates member, and contexts where member is None for other reasons crash as well). The member access needs a None guard.

Switching span sets from SET to ZSET breaks in-flight segments with WRONGTYPE errors

This changes the on-Redis type of span-buf:s:* keys from a Redis SET (sadd/sscan/scard/sunionstore) to a ZSET (zadd/zscan/zcard/zunionstore in buffer.py and add-buffer.lua) with no key versioning, draining, or dual-type handling. During a rolling deploy, keys created by old consumers are SETs; new code calling ZADD/ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZSCAN on them returns WRONGTYPE, failing process_spans/flush for those traces, and old consumers similarly fail on new ZSET keys during rollback. Buffered keys live up to redis_ttl (3600s), so in-flight segments will error and can be dropped for up to an hour around deploys.

When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, zpopmin evicts the lowest-scored (earliest end_timestamp_precise) members with no metric or log, silently discarding real span payloads rather than flagging the oversized segment as the previous flush-time check did. The evicted members can include the segment/root span (e.g. a short root span, clock skew, or a root whose children report later precise end times); the has_root_span flag computed just below still returns true because it is based on the stored flag or is_root_span of the current insert, so the now root-less segment is queued with the short root timeout and flushed as an incomplete segment. Buffer.py also removed the max_segment_spans guard in _load_segment_data (line 449), so there is no longer any flush-side detection of oversized segments produced by pre-change keys or any path that bypasses this eviction.

The test changes only add the now-required end_timestamp_precise field to existing Span constructions. Nothing exercises a segment growing past 1000 spans to verify zpopmin eviction keeps the intended (latest/root) spans, nothing verifies segments are ordered or deduplicated correctly after the SET-to-ZSET migration, and there are no tests at all for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the optimized_pagination branch in the audit-log endpoint, which currently crash on datetime keys and negative offsets. The core behavioral change of this PR is therefore unverified.

false_positives.candidate:
upsampled_count undercounts events without sample_weight

upsampled_count computes toInt64(sum(sample_weight)) with no coalesce/fallback to 1 for rows where sample_weight is NULL. Allowlisted projects can contain events predating client error sampling, events from SDKs that do not send error_sampling context, or otherwise unsampled events; for those rows sum() ignores NULLs, so a bucket containing only such events returns NULL/0 instead of its real count and mixed buckets silently undercount. The transform in error_upsampling.py applies this to every count() for allowlisted projects, so historical/normal error events disappear from charts. Use a per-row fallback such as coalesce(sample_weight, 1) before summing.

Negated or quoted event.type:error incorrectly triggers upsampling

_is_error_focused_query does a raw substring check for 'event.type:error' on the lowercased query string. A query such as '!event.type:error' (explicitly excluding errors, e.g. transaction/default events) contains that substring and returns True, as would the text inside a quoted title/message value. The endpoint then rewrites count() to sum(sample_weight), which does not exist/apply for those non-error events, producing wrong (likely zero/NULL) counts. The query needs to be parsed (or at minimum negation/quoting handled) rather than substring-matched, and spaced forms like 'event.type: error' are also missed by the current check.

Cached allowlist eligibility can go stale and be inconsistent within one request

Eligibility is cached for 60 seconds under a key built from hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))), but invalidate_upsampling_cache is never called from anywhere (option changes have no invalidation hook), so removing a project from the allowlist keeps upsampling its counts (and adding one delays it) with no bound tied to config changes. Additionally _get_event_stats re-evaluates this on every invocation, and the dashboard-split flow invokes it several times per request; a cache expiry mid-request can make the error, original, and transaction sub-queries disagree. Combined with hash() collisions between different project sets for the same organization, one set can also inherit another set's cached eligibility. Compute the decision once per request (or key the cache deterministically on the project IDs) instead of relying on an uninvalidated TTL cache.

Unlike neighbouring internal aggregates, the new SnQLFunction 'upsampled_count' in discover.py is not marked private, and transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling emits it as a user-visible column string. Any user can therefore send yAxis=upsampled_count() directly for any project/dataset, bypassing the all-projects-allowlisted gate in is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects, and get sum(sample_weight) results (NULL/0 for projects without sampling) presented as legitimate counts. Mark the function private like the other internal-only aggregates so it can only be produced by the server-side rewrite.

Mode 3 therefore can leave legacy permanently diverged from unified storage; legacy writes need to be serialised/queued per resource or otherwise ordered.

Async legacy calls race on objects shared with the returned response

Create passes the same `obj` pointer to Storage.Create and then to the background Legacy.Create while returning `created` to the caller, and Update passes the same `objInfo` (line 139) to both Storage.Update and the background Legacy.Update. This is a data race and can make the legacy copy differ from the object written to unified storage; the legacy goroutine needs its own deep copy / the precomputed updated object (as the previous updateWrapper approach provided).

In Create, when d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) with the storage start time, and Update does the same at line 129. These should call recordStorageDuration. Conversely DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration for the legacy call, the mirror-image mistake.

Legacy write failures are never logged

The background goroutines in Create, Delete (line 112), Update (line 139) and DeleteCollection (line 165) discard the legacy error except for a duration metric; the previous synchronous implementation logged these errors. Combined with the fire-and-forget design, an operator has no log signal (with kind/name) that legacy has diverged from unified storage and no way to know which objects need reconciliation. The error branch should log via the request-scoped logger before recording the metric.

Mode 3 tests never verify the async legacy write happens

The Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection tests register legacy mock expectations but return and assert on the storage result immediately, without waiting for the spawned goroutine or calling AssertExpectations/AssertCalled on the legacy mock (both mocks also share a single testify mock.Mock, so expectations cannot even distinguish the two stores). The tests pass even if the legacy write is removed entirely, and if the goroutine fires after the test finishes it can race with later tests using the shared mock and shared example objects. Tests need a synchronisation point (channel/WaitGroup in the mock or Eventually-style assertion) proving legacy is invoked with the right arguments.
