`translate` only loads `config.locale`, not the fallback locales configured in `FallbackLocaleList`. The reschedule caller in handleNewBooking.ts relies on this path and does not delete the old booking's reminders via cascade, so the old row remains scheduled=true/cancelled=null; the cron job only retries rows with cancelled=true, so if the SendGrid request throws (the error is only logged inside this function) nothing ever retries the cancellation and the old booking's reminder email is still sent. It also leaves stale scheduled reminder rows attached to the superseded booking until their scheduledDate passes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that the immediateDelete path fails to delete the WorkflowReminder database record or mark it cancelled, leaving stale active records. The candidate adds retry consequences and does not mention the omitted SendGrid DELETE call, but it matches the central underlying bug.

false_positives.candidate:
One failed SendGrid cancellation aborts cancellation of all remaining reminders

The entire cancellation loop is wrapped in a single try/catch and each SendGrid request is awaited inside it. If cancelling one reminder fails (for example an invalid or already-cancelled batch_id), the exception exits the loop, the remaining reminders in the next-hour window are never sent a cancellation request, and the Prisma delete operations already queued in workflowRemindersToDelete are never awaited (they are lazy Prisma promises), so even successfully-cancelled reminders keep their rows. Those uncancelled SendGrid emails will still be delivered for cancelled/rescheduled bookings. Each reminder needs its own error handling so one failure does not block the rest.

Last-minute cancellations are deleted without ever cancelling the SendGrid email

Deferred cancellation only happens when the cron job runs and finds cancelled=true with scheduledDate within the next hour, but at the top of the same handler all EMAIL workflowReminders with scheduledDate <= now are deleted unconditionally before the cancellation block runs. If a booking is cancelled after the last cron run before its reminder's send time (the PR states the cron runs every 15 minutes), the next run can cross the scheduledDate, delete the DB row first, and never issue the SendGrid cancel for that batch; SendGrid has already dispatched the email. The reminder for a just-cancelled booking is therefore still sent in this window, and the row deletion removes any chance of a later retry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.

Guest list has no uniqueness or size limit on the server

Direct API callers can submit duplicate addresses, duplicates differing only by case, or an arbitrarily large array; the client-side uniqueness refine in AddGuestsDialog does not protect the API. The handler's duplicate and blacklist checks are also case-sensitive for the submitted guest (the blacklist is lowercased, the guest is not), so createMany can insert duplicate attendees and the mutation can be used to fan out unbounded calendar updates and emails.
true_positives.reasoning: Although the candidate also discusses duplicates and size limits, it explicitly identifies the same blacklist bug: the blacklist is lowercased but submitted guest emails are not, making the blacklist check case-sensitive and allowing uppercase-email bypasses.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

isTeamAdminOrOwner is computed with `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`, so a team admin who is not the owner, or an owner who is not also returned as an admin, fails the check. Unless the caller is also the organizer or an attendee, legitimate team admins/owners are incorrectly rejected with FORBIDDEN. The two role checks should be combined with OR.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same permission-check bug: using AND requires the user to be both a team admin and owner, whereas OR should allow either role.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.

The handler filters submissions into uniqueGuests (removing people already on the booking and blacklisted addresses) and persists only those, but then calls sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests) with the original list. In email-manager, any attendee whose email is in that list is sent AttendeeScheduledEmail instead of AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, so an existing attendee who was resubmitted receives a fresh scheduled/invitation email rather than the guests-added notification. Pass uniqueGuests so email selection matches the attendees actually added.

The candidate additionally explains the filtering context and proposes passing uniqueGuests.

true_positives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Guest list has no uniqueness or size limit on the server

ZAddGuestsInputSchema only requires each entry to be an email string. Direct API callers can submit duplicate addresses, duplicates differing only by case, or an arbitrarily large array; the client-side uniqueness refine in AddGuestsDialog does not protect the API. The handler's duplicate and blacklist checks are also case-sensitive for the submitted guest (the blacklist is lowercased, the guest is not), so createMany can insert duplicate attendees and the mutation can be used to fan out unbounded calendar updates and emails.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that duplicate emails within the submitted guest list are not deduplicated server-side and can cause createMany to insert duplicate attendee rows. This matches the golden issue, despite additional concerns about case sensitivity and list size.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

sendAddGuestsEmails always sends organizer, team-member, and attendee emails and accepts no eventTypeMetadata, unlike the neighboring location-change/scheduled flows which honor metadata.disableStandardEmails for hosts and attendees. The addGuests handler also does not pass booking.eventType.metadata. Event types that have disabled standard emails will still emit this new set of emails.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that sendAddGuestsEmails fails to honor EventType metadata.disableStandardEmails, causing host and attendee emails to be sent even when standard emails are disabled.

false_positives.candidate:
Any attendee can add arbitrary guests to a booking

The authorization accepts anyone whose email appears in booking.attendees. An invited guest can therefore call this mutation directly to add unlimited arbitrary people to the organizer's booking, causing database attendees, calendar updates, and invitation emails to be created in the organizer's name. The new UI is on the organizer's bookings page, so attendee access is an unnecessary privilege expansion; only the organizer and authorized team admins/owners should be able to modify the guest list.

Calendar is updated with the caller's credentials instead of the organizer's

EventManager is constructed from ctx.user and getUsersCredentials(ctx.user). When the caller is a team admin/owner or another authorized user who is not the booking organizer, the calendar event is updated using the caller's credentials (or fails to find the organizer's calendar), even though the handler loads booking.user with credentials/destinationCalendar. The guests are already persisted before this step, so the database and the organizer's calendar can diverge.

Guests can be added to cancelled, rejected, or past bookings

The handler checks authorization but never checks booking.status or booking.endTime before creating attendees, calling updateCalendarAttendees, and sending scheduled/add-guests emails. A cancelled, rejected, or already-finished booking can therefore gain new attendees and trigger fresh calendar invitations and emails as if it were still an upcoming confirmed event. The server should reject non-confirmed or past bookings, not only rely on which actions the list UI happens to render.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-code login is case-sensitive while codes are presented as uppercase-style codes

Backup codes are generated as lowercase hex in the setup endpoint, displayed/copyable as XXXXX-XXXXX, and this login check only strips '-' before doing backupCodes.indexOf(...). If a user transcribes a valid code in uppercase (a-f become A-F), or an authenticator/backup note uppercases it, indexOf returns -1 and a valid single-use code is rejected with IncorrectBackupCode. The lookup should normalize the submitted code (e.g. trim and toLowerCase) before comparison.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: indexOf performs case-sensitive backup-code matching, causing valid codes entered with uppercase hex characters to be rejected. The candidate also suggests normalizing case before comparison.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Single-use backup codes can be replayed concurrently

Authorize reads user.backupCodes, checks indexOf, then later does a separate prisma.user.update setting backupCodes[index] = null. There is no atomic/conditional update or transaction locking the row between check and consumption. Two parallel login attempts using the same backup code can both read the pre-consumption array, both pass indexOf, and both be authenticated before either update lands, violating the documented 'each backup code can be used exactly once' guarantee. Consumption must be atomic (e.g. conditional update/transaction) so only one request can claim a code.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: concurrent login requests can read and validate the same backup code before its consumption is persisted, allowing a one-time code to be accepted more than once.

false_positives.candidate:
Disabling 2FA with a backup code has the same case-sensitivity bug

This endpoint computes backupCodes.indexOf(req.body.backupCode.replaceAll('-', '')) without lowercasing/trimming. A correctly transcribed backup code entered in uppercase therefore returns IncorrectBackupCode, so a user who has lost their authenticator cannot disable 2FA with a valid code. Normalize the input the same way codes are generated/stored before checking membership.

Parent is only notified of enabled 2FA when the backup-code Close button is clicked

On successful enable, handleEnable now only advances to DisplayBackupCodes instead of calling onEnable(). onEnable() is invoked solely from the backup-codes Close button. If the user dismisses the dialog via the Dialog's onOpenChange path (X button, outside click, Escape) after the server has already set twoFactorEnabled=true, the parent/security page is never refreshed and resetState() is not run, leaving the UI showing 2FA as disabled (and stale secret/backup-code state in the modal) until a full reload. The dialog-close path should perform the same completion/cleanup as the Close button.

External IdP users in the totpEmail flow cannot reach the backup-code option

When totpEmail is present (the flow used for Google/SAML users who have 2FA enabled), the footer is ExternalTotpFooter, which only offers Cancel, instead of TwoFactorFooter which contains the 'Lost access' toggle. The BackupCode form is rendered only when twoFactorLostAccess becomes true, and that state can never be set in this flow, even though the credentials authorize callback now supports backupCode. External-IdP 2FA users who lost their authenticator therefore still have no backup-code login path.

Users who enabled 2FA before this feature can never obtain backup codes

Setup returns TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled for anyone with twoFactorEnabled=true, and this PR adds no regenerate/view endpoint or settings action. All pre-existing 2FA users therefore have backupCodes=null forever unless they disable and re-enable 2FA; if they try a backup code at login they get MissingBackupCodes, whose message says 'Please generate them in your settings' even though no such settings action exists. Add a regeneration flow for already-enabled users or change the message/flow so these users are not dead-ended.

No test exercises actually logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code

The added e2e coverage only clicks the backup-code download/copy buttons and checks the filename/toast during setup; the file itself notes 'TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup'. The security-critical new behavior — valid backup code logs in, the same code cannot be reused, an invalid code is rejected, and a backup code can disable 2FA — is entirely untested, so regressions in next-auth-options.ts or disable.ts would not be caught.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

The code destructures `evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` into `mainHostDestinationCalendar` and then accesses `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. When destinationCalendar is null, undefined, or an empty array (handleNewBooking explicitly sets it to null when neither the event type nor organizer has one), this throws a TypeError during EventManager.create, breaking booking creation instead of falling back to Cal Video.

The candidate describes the booking-creation impact but does not mention updateEvent; this does not change the underlying issue.

Previously this returned destinationCalendar.externalId. Updates therefore call Google with an undefined calendarId and deletes fall back to "primary", so reschedules/cancellations for events stored on a non-primary destination calendar fail or target the wrong calendar.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the faulty destination-calendar lookup comparing cal.externalId to externalCalendarId, which fails to select the intended calendar. The candidate clarifies the falsy-ID fallback branch and its consequences, but addresses the same underlying logic error.

This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled

Non-Google calendar services still create collective events only on the first host's calendar

For the second and later hosts it therefore tries to write to the main host's externalId with another user's token, causing failures or events in the wrong calendar; it should select the destination whose credentialId matches the instance's credential (Google does this via the new credentialId argument).

updateLocation now creates booking references without calendar/credential IDs

updateLocation builds referencesToCreate from `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId`, but CalendarManager.updateEvent's returned EventResult (CalendarManager.ts:313-322) never sets either field. Previously these came from evt.destinationCalendar. Edit-location therefore persists BookingReference rows with externalCalendarId and credentialId undefined, losing the link needed by later reschedule, update, and cancellation flows to target the correct external calendar.

The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async forEach makes calendar/video cancellation fire-and-forget and bypasses try/catch

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) })` discards the promises returned by the callback. Reschedule() can return true and the reschedule email can be sent before deletions finish, deletions can be lost on process termination, and a rejection from the now-async getCalendar/deleteMeeting is not caught by the surrounding try/catch (which only catches synchronous throws), producing an unhandled rejection instead of the logged error. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` inside the try.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify async callbacks in forEach whose promises are discarded, causing fire-and-forget cleanup, unhandled rejections that bypass surrounding try/catch, and completion before deletions finish. The candidate also proposes the same Promise.all with map fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are all executed eagerly, not lazily per app

Every value in the appStore object literal is an import() call, so merely importing packages/app-store/index.ts immediately starts loading all ~30 app modules; accessing appStore.zoomvideo does not lazily load only Zoom. This defeats the stated goal of async/lazy app loading, keeps the startup/bundle cost the PR aims to remove, and creates stored promises for apps that are never used (including possible unhandled rejections if an unused app fails to load). Values should be thunks such as `zoomvideo: () => import("./zoomvideo")` and call sites should invoke then await them.

requestReschedule does not await calendar/video deletions

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) / deleteMeeting(...) })` discards the async callback promises. The mutation proceeds to send the reschedule email and webhooks and returns without guaranteeing the old calendar/video events were deleted, and any rejection from getCalendar/deleteEvent/deleteMeeting becomes an unhandled rejection rather than being surfaced or logged. Replace forEach with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hung spawn flusher is never killed before being replaced

Flusher workers are created with multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, whose objects are SpawnProcess/BaseProcess instances, not instances of multiprocessing.Process. The isinstance check therefore never passes in production, so a worker detected as hung is not killed before _create_process_for_shards starts its replacement. The hung worker can keep polling and flushing the same Redis shards concurrently with the new worker, causing duplicate buffered-segment production and races between flush_segments/done_flush_segments, while the reference to the leaked worker is overwritten in self.processes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug. Spawn-context processes are SpawnProcess instances, not multiprocessing.Process instances, so the isinstance check fails and hung processes are not killed.

false_positives.candidate:
join() never terminates spawn flusher processes

For the same reason as the restart path, isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is false for processes created through the spawn context (and for the threading.Thread workers used when produce_to_pipe is set, terminate is inapplicable). After join() waits until its deadline for workers that ignore the shared stopped flag, the terminate call is skipped, so shutdown can return while daemon flusher processes are still alive flushing segments and producing to Kafka; they are only cleaned up implicitly when the parent process exits.

Invalid --flusher-processes values are silently remapped or crash obscurely

The CLI option added for process-spans accepts any integer and SpanFlusher performs no positive-value validation. Passing 0 is silently changed by `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` into one process per shard, the opposite of an operator's explicit request, while a negative value makes num_processes negative, builds an empty process_to_shards_map, and then fails with a KeyError on `i % self.num_processes` during shard assignment instead of a clear configuration error at startup.

This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

The candidate also raises a separate point about neither field being present, but that does not change the match.

Error events are interleaved using mismatched timestamp units

After credentialManager().isValid() succeeds, this code only checks RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.allCodesUsed() on the fetched credential. For a local credential, Keycloak's recovery-code provider consumes the code as part of validation and persists that state; for a federated credential, validation is delegated to the user storage's CredentialInputValidator, which merely validates the input (as the test provider does) and does not update the hashed code list or its used flags. Nothing here calls updateCredential/disableCredentialType to persist consumption. Consequently the same federated recovery code can be reused indefinitely, and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean will keep asking for the first unused code instead of advancing to the next code.

Exhausted federated recovery credentials are not removed

When allCodesUsed() is true, the code calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(...). That operation removes credentials from Keycloak's local credential store only; it does not delete or disable a credential owned by a federated user storage. Because getCredential() now preferentially returns the federated credential, an exhausted federated credential can remain configured after this call while a CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is also added, leaving stale/used codes in the external storage and potentially causing repeated setup or inconsistent configuredFor state.

Raw recovery codes are sent to user storage instead of the hashed credential data

credentialModel already contains the recovery codes in Keycloak's hashed credential representation, but createRecoveryCodesCredential discards that data and sends JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes), i.e. the plaintext codes, as the UserCredentialModel challenge response. A federated provider that persists the challenge response verbatim (the added BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage does exactly that) will store usable recovery codes in plaintext, unlike local storage which stores hashes. Compromise of the federated store would therefore disclose valid recovery codes; the helper should pass the hashed credential data or clearly require/implement hashing in the storage contract.

Federated recovery credential loses user label and generation time

The UserCredentialModel sent to user storage is constructed only from credentialModel.getType() and the generated-code JSON. It does not carry credentialModel's userLabel or createdDate/generation time, even though RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(generatedCodes, generatedAtTime, generatedUserLabel) was built with those values in RecoveryAuthnCodesAction. Federated providers therefore cannot persist the label/date chosen at setup; the test provider substitutes the current time and a null label, so account/console displays and credential metadata for federated recovery codes will be wrong or empty.

Federated recovery-code test does not verify single-use or code advancement

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin logs in once with the code at index 0 and logs out. It does not attempt to reuse the same code, log in again with the next code, verify that the login page requests the next code number, or verify behavior when all codes are exhausted. Those are the main behavioral differences between local hashed recovery credentials and federated validation, so the current test would pass even though federated codes remain replayable and never advance.

Every existing implementation outside the three updated in this PR (custom server providers, downstream/client-repo implementations, mocks and test doubles) will fail to compile until it adds order(). This is an avoidable source/binary contract break for an ordering feature: order() should be a default method with a documented default priority, with built-in providers overriding it as needed.

Equal-order providers are silently and nondeterministically selected instead of rejected

detectProvider() sorts by order() descending and unconditionally returns the first provider. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so when more than one is on the classpath the winner depends on ServiceLoader encounter/classpath order. Previously this configuration failed fast with 'Multiple crypto providers loaded'; now Keycloak can silently run with DefaultCryptoProvider instead of the FIPS provider (or vice versa), defeating an operator's explicit FIPS configuration and hiding a misconfiguration. Ties for the highest order should remain an error, or the mutually exclusive full providers need distinct, intentional priorities.

ECDSA test never verifies the produced DER signature and does not test provider ordering

test() only checks DER->RS->DER->RS self-consistency using the same custom ASN.1 encoder/decoder pair, and generates a single default EC key pair regardless of whether ES256, ES384 or ES512 is under test. A mutually compensating encoder/decoder defect, or DER that JCA rejects, would still pass, and the central new behaviour of this PR (CryptoIntegration choosing between AuthzClientCryptoProvider order 100 and a full provider order 200, including tie handling) has no test at all. The test should verify asn1Des with Signature.verify() using a curve-appropriate key pair, and CryptoIntegration selection should be covered directly.

false_positives.candidate:
Queues are unbounded despite claimed backpressure

FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with the default maxsize=0 (unbounded), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() never blocks or rejects. The docstring at lines 253-254 promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but under a slow result_processor the Arroyo processor will keep submitting messages indefinitely, growing memory without bound and building a huge outstanding-offset set (also delaying commits past max.poll.interval). Bound the queues and make submit() apply backpressure, or remove the claim and add another flow-control mechanism.

Shutdown abandons queued-but-unprocessed items

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True for every worker before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker.run() re-checks `while not self.shutdown` after each item, so a worker that finishes its current item exits even if its queue still holds pending items (which immediate=False was supposed to drain). Those items are never processed and their offsets stay outstanding forever in this process; graceful shutdown silently drops in-flight work (only redelivery on restart saves it, and only if offsets were not already marked complete). Don't set the flag until queues are drained, or have workers exit only when the queue is empty and shut down.

close() stops the commit loop before workers drain

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread first, and only then calls queue_pool.shutdown(). Any items the workers finish during pool shutdown therefore complete their offsets after the last _commit_loop iteration, so those offsets are never passed to commit_function. Arroyo will consider the strategy closed and will not poll again, so successfully processed messages are redelivered and reprocessed on restart. Drain the pool first (and run a final commit pass), then stop the commit thread.

Queue pool is created once in the factory but killed by each strategy close

FixedQueuePool is constructed a single time in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ (line 133) and the same instance is handed to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy from create_with_partitions(). Arroyo calls create_with_partitions() again after a rebalance/revocation, but the previous strategy's close()/terminate() calls queue_pool.shutdown(), which shuts down the shared queues and joins the workers. The next strategy reuses that dead pool: work_queue.put() raises queue.ShutDown, which SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() catches and converts into add_offset+complete_offset, so messages are silently dropped yet committed. Create a fresh pool per create_with_partitions() call (or make the pool restartable and don't shut it down in strategy close).

submit() marks messages complete and committable on any error

The bare `except Exception` in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() logs and then does add_offset()+complete_offset() for the message regardless of where the failure occurred - e.g. grouping_fn raising, or FixedQueuePool.submit() failing after add_offset() when putting onto a shut-down queue. Combined with OrderedQueueWorker.run() completing offsets in its `finally` block even when result_processor raises (line 148-149), this contradicts the documented 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and turns transient/poison failures into committed, never-retried message loss instead of letting Arroyo/DLQ handle them. Only skip-and-commit for explicitly undecodable/filtered payloads; propagate or leave outstanding other failures.

Kafka commit function is invoked from a background thread

_commit_loop runs on a dedicated daemon thread and calls self.commit_function(committable) (which is Arroyo's Commit callable built in create_thread_queue_parallel_worker) concurrently with the StreamProcessor main thread that owns submit()/poll()/close(). Arroyo commit callbacks are expected to be invoked from the processing thread during submit/poll/join; racing them against processor-driven commits and shutdown can corrupt/interleave offset state and commit offsets for partitions that have since been revoked. Perform commits from poll() on the strategy thread, using the tracker only to compute committable offsets.

Committable-offset scan is O(range) every second per partition

get_committable_offsets() runs min()/max() over the full all_offsets set and then iterates range(start, max_offset+1) with set lookups, and mark_committed() rebuilds the whole set - all repeated every 1s by _commit_loop for every partition. With a backlog (made likely by the unbounded queues), a single slow offset pins a large outstanding set, so each tick rescans an ever-growing range, giving quadratic behaviour and burning a thread. Track the next-expected offset and a completed set per partition instead of rescanning the whole window.

hash() is not a stable consistent hash for group assignment

get_queue_for_group() uses Python's builtin hash(group_key) % num_queues and documents it as 'consistent hashing'. For str keys hash() is randomised per process via PYTHONHASHSEED, so the group->queue mapping changes on every restart and differs between concurrently running consumer processes; it is also a plain modulo, so changing num_queues (--max-workers) remaps nearly every group. This defeats any cross-restart/cross-process affinity expectations and makes queue distribution non-reproducible in tests/operations. Use a stable digest (e.g. hashlib.md5/sha1 of the key) modulo num_queues.

wait_until_empty reports empty while items are still being processed

wait_until_empty() (and poll()'s total_queued gauge) rely on queue.qsize(), but OrderedQueueWorker removes an item from the queue via get() before it starts processing it. The method therefore returns True while the last item(s) - one per queue - are still in-flight and their offsets not yet completed, so any caller using it as a drain/flush barrier (as shutdown-style tests do) can proceed/commit/tear down too early. Track in-flight counts (e.g. queue.task_done()/join() or an explicit counter incremented on submit and decremented in the worker's finally).

false_positives.candidate:
Switching span sets from SET to ZSET breaks in-flight segments with WRONGTYPE errors

This changes the on-Redis type of span-buf:s:* keys from a Redis SET (sadd/sscan/scard/sunionstore) to a ZSET (zadd/zscan/zcard/zunionstore in buffer.py and add-buffer.lua) with no key versioning, draining, or dual-type handling. The evicted members can include the segment/root span (e.g. a short root span, clock skew, or a root whose children report later precise end times); the has_root_span flag computed just below still returns true because it is based on the stored flag or is_root_span of the current insert, so the now root-less segment is queued with the short root timeout and flushed as an incomplete segment. Buffer.py also removed the max_segment_spans guard in _load_segment_data (line 449), so there is no longer any flush-side detection of oversized segments produced by pre-change keys or any path that bypasses this eviction.

The test changes only add the now-required end_timestamp_precise field to existing Span constructions. Nothing exercises a segment growing past 1000 spans to verify zpopmin eviction keeps the intended (latest/root) spans, nothing verifies segments are ordered or deduplicated correctly after the SET-to-ZSET migration, and there are no tests at all for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the optimized_pagination branch in the audit-log endpoint, which currently crash on datetime keys and negative offsets. upsampled_count undercounts events without sample_weight

upsampled_count computes toInt64(sum(sample_weight)) with no coalesce/fallback to 1 for rows where sample_weight is NULL. Allowlisted projects can contain events predating client error sampling, events from SDKs that do not send error_sampling context, or otherwise unsampled events; for those rows sum() ignores NULLs, so a bucket containing only such events returns NULL/0 instead of its real count and mixed buckets silently undercount. The transform in error_upsampling.py applies this to every count() for allowlisted projects, so historical/normal error events disappear from charts. Use a per-row fallback such as coalesce(sample_weight, 1) before summing.

Negated or quoted event.type:error incorrectly triggers upsampling

_is_error_focused_query does a raw substring check for 'event.type:error' on the lowercased query string. A query such as '!event.type:error' (explicitly excluding errors, e.g. transaction/default events) contains that substring and returns True, as would the text inside a quoted title/message value. The endpoint then rewrites count() to sum(sample_weight), which does not exist/apply for those non-error events, producing wrong (likely zero/NULL) counts. The query needs to be parsed (or at minimum negation/quoting handled) rather than substring-matched, and spaced forms like 'event.type: error' are also missed by the current check.

Additionally _get_event_stats re-evaluates this on every invocation, and the dashboard-split flow invokes it several times per request; a cache expiry mid-request can make the error, original, and transaction sub-queries disagree. Combined with hash() collisions between different project sets for the same organization, one set can also inherit another set's cached eligibility. Compute the decision once per request (or key the cache deterministically on the project IDs) instead of relying on an uninvalidated TTL cache.

upsampled_count is exposed as a public function for non-allowlisted projects

Unlike neighbouring internal aggregates, the new SnQLFunction 'upsampled_count' in discover.py is not marked private, and transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling emits it as a user-visible column string. false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the cancelled request context

Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection all launch `go func()` blocks that derive their timeout with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` from the incoming request context. The Kubernetes request context is cancelled as soon as the handler returns the storage result, which happens immediately after spawning the goroutine, so the legacy write will almost always run with an already-cancelled context and fail/abandon. A detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) before adding the timeout) is required, otherwise mode 3 silently does not perform the legacy writes it exists to perform as a safety net.

Independent goroutines give no ordering for legacy writes

Every write spawns an unsynchronised goroutine for the legacy store. A Create goroutine, a subsequent Update goroutine and a Delete goroutine for the same object can be scheduled or complete out of order (legacy latency is variable up to the 10s timeout): an update can run before the create it depends on and fail as not-found, or a delayed create can run after a delete and resurrect a deleted object in legacy storage. Mode 3 therefore can leave legacy permanently diverged from unified storage; legacy writes need to be serialised/queued per resource or otherwise ordered.

Async legacy calls race on objects shared with the returned response

Create passes the same `obj` pointer to Storage.Create and then to the background Legacy.Create while returning `created` to the caller, and Update passes the same `objInfo` (line 139) to both Storage.Update and the background Legacy.Update. The API server may serialise/mutate the returned object, and UpdatedObjectInfo.UpdatedObject may be invoked a second time against a different old object, concurrently with the first call and with response handling. This is a data race and can make the legacy copy differ from the object written to unified storage; the legacy goroutine needs its own deep copy / the precomputed updated object (as the previous updateWrapper approach provided).

Storage failures are recorded as legacy metrics

In Create, when d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) with the storage start time, and Update does the same at line 129. Storage failures are therefore attributed to the legacy duration metric (with the wrong latency) and no failing storage duration is recorded, corrupting the dual-writer dashboards/alerts used to judge migration safety. These should call recordStorageDuration. Conversely DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration for the legacy call, the mirror-image mistake.

Legacy write failures are never logged

The background goroutines in Create, Delete (line 112), Update (line 139) and DeleteCollection (line 165) discard the legacy error except for a duration metric; the previous synchronous implementation logged these errors. Combined with the fire-and-forget design, an operator has no log signal (with kind/name) that legacy has diverged from unified storage and no way to know which objects need reconciliation. The error branch should log via the request-scoped logger before recording the metric.

Mode 3 tests never verify the async legacy write happens

The Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection tests register legacy mock expectations but return and assert on the storage result immediately, without waiting for the spawned goroutine or calling AssertExpectations/AssertCalled on the legacy mock (both mocks also share a single testify mock.Mock, so expectations cannot even distinguish the two stores). The tests pass even if the legacy write is removed entirely, and if the goroutine fires after the test finishes it can race with later tests using the shared mock and shared example objects. Tests need a synchronisation point (channel/WaitGroup in the mock or Eventually-style assertion) proving legacy is invoked with the right arguments.

New mode 3 integration cases are flaky because legacy visibility is now asynchronous

The added 'mode 3' subtests reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates/updates/deletes via the k8s API and then immediately asserts the objects are visible (and later gone) through the legacy /api/playlists endpoints. In mode 3 the legacy write is performed by a fire-and-forget goroutine started before the response returns, so there is no guarantee it has completed when the very next legacy request is made. These subtests will intermittently fail (missing/extra/stale playlists) unless the legacy assertions poll/wait for eventual consistency.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are not loaded before cached translation lookup

`translate` only loads `config.locale`, not the fallback locales configured in `FallbackLocaleList`. Outside `ApplicationController#set_locale` (background jobs, mailers, console, or translations before that filter) a key missing from the current locale will be looked up in fallback locales whose YAML files have never been loaded via the lazy-loading patch, so it returns a missing-translation string. Worse, the no-argument path stores that result in the LRU cache (`@cache.getset(k) { translate_no_cache(key).freeze }`), so the missing string stays cached under `key+locale` even after the fallback locale is later loaded, until eviction/reload. Fallbacks must be ensured-loaded inside `translate` (or the backend lookup) before computing/caching the value, and the cache must not persist results computed before fallback locales were loaded.

Fallback loading is only wired into web requests

The PR is described as server-side localization fallbacks, but `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is only invoked from `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Server-side code that sets `I18n.locale` and translates without going through this controller (Sidekiq jobs, mailers, rake tasks, plugin background work) never loads the site-default/English fallback files, so with the lazy translation loader those fallbacks silently return missing translations there. The ensure-loaded step belongs in the shared translation path (e.g. `I18n.translate`/`load_locale` logic), not solely in a controller filter.

Fallback lookup queries SiteSetting on every translation

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` is called by the I18n fallbacks backend on every translation lookup, and it calls `SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym` each time. That puts a site-setting lookup (backed by Discourse's setting provider/cache machinery) on the hottest possible path — the very path `translate_accelerator.rb` exists to optimize — and it also raises `NoMethodError` if `default_locale` is ever nil/blank (e.g. early boot or a cleared setting). The fallback chain should be computed without a per-lookup setting query, or at minimum memoized/guarded with a safe default such as `:en`.

No tests cover the custom fallback chain or its lazy loading

This PR introduces a custom `FallbackLocaleList`, replaces the Rails `config.i18n.fallbacks` mechanism, removes the standalone pluralization initializer, and adds `I18n.ensure_loaded!`, but adds no specs. There is nothing verifying that a key missing in the user locale falls back to the site default and then English, that fallback locale files actually get loaded under the lazy-loading patch (including outside controllers), or that pluralized fallback strings still work. Regressions in this global I18n behavior would only surface as missing-translation strings in production; add specs for the fallback order, loading, and a pluralized fallback lookup before merging.

If an originally public imported topic is later moved into a restricted category, made invisible, or otherwise access-controlled, anonymous visitors framing the embed from the allowed host can still read its best posts through /embed/best.

Import first queries TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first and only later creates the row inside a block, while the migration adds a unique index on embed_url. Two concurrent retrievals or feed polls for the same new URL can both see no embed, both create topics/posts, and then one fails with RecordNotUnique on TopicEmbed.create!, rolling back or orphaning work after external effects/jobs have been enqueued. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Percentage downsize breaks animated GIF handling

The controller calls OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails). When allow_animation is true and the file is a GIF, OptimizedImage.optimize dispatches to downsize_instructions_animated/resize_instructions_animated, which passes the dimensions to gifsicle as --resize-fit. Gifsicle expects WxH dimensions, not "80%" (the value also gets a trailing \> from the non-animated path conventions), so it will fail to resize animated GIFs. The loop then retries the failing operation up to 5 times and the oversized GIF proceeds to Upload.create_for still over the limit, so large animated uploads are not actually downsized.

If convert/gifsicle fails (corrupt image, unsupported format such as SVG, unsupported geometry), convert_with returns false but the loop still runs up to 5 expensive attempts and then uploads whatever is left at that path. Assigning notification_level and calling tu.save! skips the logic in TopicUser.change that stamps notifications_changed_at, sets notifications_reason_id to user_changed, observes after-save callbacks, and publishes a MessageBus notification_level_change. Other open clients therefore keep showing the old notification state and the change is not recorded consistently with every other notification-level change in the app. Call TopicUser.change(current_user.id, topic_id, notification_level: ...) instead.

First click does not actually stop notifications for watching/tracking users

If notification_level is above regular (watching or tracking), the action only downgrades it to regular, not muted. A regular user still receives mention/quote/reply notifications for the topic, so the email promise 'To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here' and the landing page text 'You will stop receiving notifications' are false after the click the email invites; the user must discover and operate the extra dropdown to finish unsubscribing.

The shared unsubscribe_link string now interpolates %{unsubscribe_url}, and Email::MessageBuilder passes template_args to I18n.t whenever add_unsubscribe_link is true (in both body and html_part). I18n raises MissingInterpolationArgument when a key is absent, so any current or plugin mailer that sets add_unsubscribe_link: true without also passing unsubscribe_url (previously a valid, working combination) will now crash while building email. Only include the per-topic sentence when unsubscribe_url is present, or supply a default in MessageBuilder.

The only spec change adds unsubscribe_url to an existing MessageBuilder fixture, but the examples still assert only the user-preferences URL and List-Unsubscribe header; nothing asserts the per-topic URL actually appears in text/HTML bodies, and there is no controller spec for TopicsController#unsubscribe at all (level transitions watching->?, regular->muted, missing TopicUser row, wrong slug redirect, logged-out user).
